"There is. If one has previously performed the ritual of pure giving (*viśuddha-dāna*) for another and then eats while ill, there is no offense.
If one accepts food from relatives at various places, there is no offense."
If a bhikṣu has accepted an invitation to eat, and food is offered to him at his seat or elsewhere, he commits no offense if he resolves not to accept the food.
If a bhikṣu has accepted an invitation, and someone says:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"If there will be more food, I shall not invite the Venerable One.
If he eats [under these conditions], he does not commit an offense.

If a bhikṣu accepts two kinds of invitations—namely, for *khādaniya* (solid food) and *bhojaniya* (soft food)—but they have not been formally offered (*pariṇata*), and he eats them, he does not commit an offense.
After a bhikṣu has already accepted an invitation, someone says:
"Venerable sir, please take note!
I have food, but I did not invite you."
"Those who eat do not commit an offense.
After a bhikṣu has already accepted an invitation, someone says:
'Venerable Sir!'"
"I have food appropriate for the illness; I did not invite the Venerable One.
In such a case, the one who eats commits no offense.
"Is there a case where a bhikṣu accepts an invitation from two places, and though the gift is impure, he commits no offense?"
He replied:
"There is, provided it is not solid food."
There was a bhikṣu who had already accepted an invitation, when someone said to him:
"Venerable sir!
You have come to my house, yet I did not invite you."
There is no offense for one who eats.
There is no offense for one who eats among those seated if they were not previously invited.
There is no offense for one who eats if there is another person invited to that same seat.
There is no offense in accepting food from one who has been invited regularly.
There is no offense in accepting food out of compassion.

Regarding "extra food" (*adhika-bhaktam*): if, at a layperson’s house, food is prepared early in the morning and a portion for a renunciant is set aside before eating, this is called extra food. Accepting such food is not an offense.
One who eats this food does not commit the offense of eating with two people; if one person takes both portions together and they are consumed as a single unit, the eater commits no offense.
To receive impure food by means of a hand-gesture (mudrā) constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a madman comes to invite one, and because of doubt one accepts another invitation instead, there is no offense.
If a mad bhikṣu accepts an invitation for a meal, and a bhikṣu who has received the method of "pure giving" (pariṇāmanā) eats it, there is no offense.
He made twenty-one prostrations.
The lay devotee said to the bhikṣu,
"Venerable sir, please accept my invitation."
"If that bhikṣu accepts food through an improper distribution, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
[The questioner asks: "Is there any situation where one might accept invitations for meals from two families in one place without committing an offense?
The answer is:
“There are. Namely, food from a nāga palace, food from a deva shrine, and food from non-Buddhist practitioners.
“Is there any case where a bhikṣu may accept two or three bowls of food without committing an offense?”
He replied: “There are.
It is not an offense in the case of non-Buddhist sects, celestial shrines, or yakṣa shrines.”
To receive [food] by means of a hand-seal (mudrā) constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This does not constitute an offense when receiving cakes or similar items as "remaining food" (*vighasa*).
If one takes more than two or three bowls and has another person carry them away, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
“Is there a case where a bhikṣu, having finished eating and being invited to eat more, may eat again without violating the rule regarding the refusal of leftover food?
Answer: “There is.”
If one is ill, ghee and honey are treated in the same way.
If, after having eaten impure food, one partakes of a further portion at will under the rule for "leftover food," this is not considered "receiving food"; it is a *pāyattika*.
"What is impure food?
It refers to a formal meal.

Is there a case where a bhikṣu, having finished eating at his pleasure, eats again without having received the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the 'leftover-food' procedure), yet does not commit a *pāyattika* offense?"
Answer: "There is.
If one stays as a thief, or if one is training in the precepts, or if one was originally not in harmony, or if one originally violated the precepts, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu eats apart from the community (pṛthag-bhakta) without committing a pāyattika offense? Answer: "There is."
"If one travels more than half a yojana, there is no offense.
"As the Buddha has taught, eating separately from the community incurs no offense except for specific causes and conditions.
Are these all the causes and conditions that must be present, or is it sufficient for each individual cause and condition to be present?"
He replied:
"If one eats when each individual cause and condition is present before them, there is no offense.
Is there any case where a bhikṣu may eat apart from the community without committing an offense?"
Answer: "There is.
If one eats outside the boundary or eats in mid-air, there is no offense."
“Is there any bhikṣu who, by eating *khādaniya* or *bhojaniya* food at an improper time, does not commit an offense?
Answer: “There is.”
"If one dwells in Uttarakuru and consumes food at that time, there is no offense.
Question:
"Is it possible for a bhikṣu to commit four offenses while eating in a single sitting?"
Answer: "There is.

If one eats food that has not been formally accepted, impure food, food at the improper time, or leftover food from the previous night, one commits four *pāyattika* offenses for every mouthful that enters the mouth."
Question:
"May one eat food that was kept overnight in Uttarakuru? Answer:
"One may eat it.
It is the same in other regions as well.
There are three kinds of food stored overnight that a bhikṣu must not eat."
"What are the three? They are:
living as a thief (corāvasa), being originally unharmonious, and training in the precepts (śikṣamāṇā).
Is there any bhikṣu who, by eating leftover food, does not commit an offense?"
Answer: "There is.
If a bhikṣuṇī has kept food overnight, a bhikṣu may eat it."
If a bhikṣu has stored food, a bhikṣuṇī may eat it.
If the rim of the bowl is chipped and the remnants of food are placed in a vessel, provided that one uses the utmost care to wash away the old grease three times before eating, there is no offense.
If one gives it to a śrāmaṇera and the śrāmaṇera returns it, and the bhikṣu uses it for food, there is no offense.
If one gives leftover food to another and that person returns it, eating it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
If one does not accept food oneself, there is no offense.
If one eats using the custom of Uttarakuru, where food is not accepted, there is no offense;
this is not permitted in other regions.
If, while a bhikṣu is eating, a layperson places khādaniya or bhojaniya food into his bowl, is this considered a formal acceptance?
If it can be set aside, one should set it aside; if it cannot be set aside, one may eat it.
There is no offense in the case of turbid water, salt water, or ash-water.
"Is there any instance where one seeks fine food for oneself and yet incurs no offense? Answer:
“There is. If one requests [food] from a nāga, a yakṣa, or any non-human being, there is no offense.
“Is there any case where a bhikṣu requests fine food and yet commits no offense?”
He replied: "There is.
One may request it from one's relatives."
Water containing insects should be strained.
If one sits in a secluded place with a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch), it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one sits inside a house with a *paṇḍaka*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To sit together with one who is not one's own master in a house is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To sit in a secluded place [with such a person] is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
What is meant by "a house where one is not one's own master"?
If one sits at will within the home of parents, relatives, or others, there is no offense.
A house where there are many children and the property has not yet been divided is called a "house of non-autonomy."
If one sits among those who have already divided their property and taken wives, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one sits among those from whom the monastery’s master has been seized, or sits together with members of non-Buddhist monasteries, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu may sit together [with a woman] without committing an offense?
He replied: "There is."
"If one sits together with [a woman] in open space,
is there any case where a bhikṣu sits together with [a woman] in a secluded place and does not commit an offense? Answer:
“There is. If, within a great assembly, he sits in an unsecluded place.
“Is it possible for a bhikṣu to incur a pārājika offense by eating in a secluded place?”
He replied: "There is.
It is called the desire for food."
“Is there any case where a bhikṣu sitting in a secluded place commits a pāyattika offense? Answer: “There is.”
"Regarding the rule on forcing someone to sit:
if one eats ghee, oil, honey, or molasses in a secluded place, or drinks water containing insects, it is a pāyattika.
Is there any case where a bhikṣu uses water containing insects and does not commit an offense?"
Answer: “There is.
If one bathes therein while there is a tiger present, it is a duṣkṛta.”
"To dispatch a messenger by means of a hand-seal constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to an outsider and does not commit an offense? Answer:
“There is. If it is for a relative, or if one is ill, or if one intends to leave the household life;
yet to give food by hand signal constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.”
“Is there any case where a bhikṣu goes to watch an army on its march and does not commit a pāyattika offense? Answer: “There is.”
If one goes to observe the military expeditions of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and so forth, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
However, there is no offense if one is surrounded by the fourfold army, if summoned by the king, or if any one of the eight difficulties occurs.
Whether within a household or inside a monastery, there is no offense whatsoever.
The same applies to staying more than two nights to observe an army on its march.

If a bhikṣu strikes any of three types of persons, it is a duṣkṛta (offense of wrong-doing): namely, one who dwells as a thief, one who was originally not in harmony [with the Saṃgha], and one who originally violated the precepts.
If one throws an object at many bhikṣus, for each instance it strikes, one incurs that many pāyattikas;
if it does not strike anyone, it is a duṣkṛta.
Question:
"Is it possible for a bhikṣu to incur one hundred thousand pāyattikas through a single means? Answer:
“There is. If a bhikṣu takes sand or beans and scatters them at other bhikṣus, whether they strike them or not, it is as previously explained.
If a bhikṣu raises a hand-blade toward many bhikṣus, he incurs many pāyattikas.

If one confesses [a grave offense] to four kinds of persons, it is a *duṣkṛta*: namely, one who lives as a thief (a *corāvasatha*), one who was originally not in communion (*anupasampanna*), one who has fundamentally violated the precepts (*pārājika*), and one who is training in the precepts (*śikṣamāṇā*).
Is it not the case that concealing a grave offense from someone who is not a bhikṣu constitutes concealment?
Answer: "It does not constitute concealment.
In the dwelling place of thieves, in a place where there was originally no harmony, or in a place where one has previously broken the precepts, it is not termed 'concealment'."
If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a grave offense, and that [offender] says,
"I have not committed it," and the witness does not speak of it to others, this is not called concealment.
If a bhikṣu conceals a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) committed by another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu conceals a grave offense committed by a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
"One whose mind is deranged, insane, or distracted incurs no offense for concealing a grave transgression.
This is likewise true for the five assemblies as they revolve among one another like a wheel.
Question:
"If one confesses to a madman, does the confession become valid?
He replied,
"It does not become valid."
"Concealing a grave offense within the Saṃgha is a pāyattika.
Regarding the expulsion of a śrāmaṇera: should it be relinquished or should it not be relinquished? Answer:
"It should be relinquished.
If a śrāmaṇera confesses before the Saṃgha or confesses during the poṣadha, he should be accepted.
If a bhikṣu, at the time of the poṣadha, brings his offense to mind and discloses it, it is not called concealment.
If a bhikṣu expels a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
To expel a bhikṣu from the home of a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) is a duṣkṛta offense.
To expel a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī is a duṣkṛta offense.
To send a messenger to a non-Buddhist household to drive out a śrāmaṇera constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
To drive out a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu places ghee, oil, or honey into a fire, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If he burns bones, various old garments, or similar items, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If he burns firewood or other materials already in the fire, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu stays overnight with one who has not yet received full ordination for more than two nights without committing an offense?
Answer: "There is."
"If it is beneath a fence, a wall, or under a tree, there is no offense.
"Is it possible for a bhikṣu to stay overnight together with one who has not received full ordination for more than two nights and yet incur two pāyattikas?"
He replied: "There is.
Having stayed overnight with a śrāmaṇera for two nights, one stays overnight with a woman on the third night."
If a bhikṣu eats together with a bhikṣu who has been expelled for the purpose of purifying his offense, he incurs a pāyattika.
If he eats together with one who is insane or one whose mind is distracted for the purpose of purifying his offense, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu who has been expelled confesses his offense, it is a duṣkṛta.
A śrāmaṇera says:
"I know what the Buddha has taught: desire does not obstruct the Path."
Once the community of monks has reached harmony, if that person repents and returns, they should be accepted.
If a bhikṣu gives his consent (*chanda*) to a bhikṣu who does not accept the Dharma and subsequently reproaches him, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The same applies to cases contrary to the above.
To perform a *karmavācanā* for one who is staying as a thief (*caura-vāsika*), and then to voice a reproach after having already granted consent (*chanda*), constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.

To perform a *karmavācanā* for one under training (*śikṣamāṇā*), one who was originally not in harmony, one who originally violated the precepts, a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, and then to voice a reproach, constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
"Is there any bhikṣu who, wearing a robe of undyed color, does not commit a pāyattika offense? Answer: "There is."
To wear impure clothing—namely, *kambala* wool—is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one wears clothing that has been purified by discoloring an impure garment, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu wears a dyed robe, a bhikṣuṇī may wear it, and even a śrāmaṇerī may wear it.
If a śrāmaṇerī wears a pure (undyed) robe, a bhikṣu may wear it, and even a śrāmaṇera may wear it.
"Items such as the cloth for wiping the feet, hand towels, water filters, alms-bowl bags, and waist-bands must all be purified.
If a bhikṣu’s robe is seized by a king or a householder and is later recovered, must it be purified once again?"
He replied:
"One does not, because it has already been purified.
[The questioner asked: "Is there any case where a bhikṣu, by taking precious objects or things resembling precious objects, does not commit a pāyattika offense?"
Answer: “There is.
If one takes the treasures of devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and so forth, it is a duṣkṛta offense.”
"If one sends a messenger to fetch jewels from a certain place, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
[Question: "Is there any case where a bhikṣu takes a *maṇi* jewel and does not commit an offense? Answer:
“There is. If one takes rock crystal or *maṇi* gems, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one takes them for another with the intention [of returning them], and returns them to the owner, there is no offense.”
“Is there any case where a bhikṣu sits or lies upon a bed made of gold and jewels without committing an offense?
He replied: “There is.”
"If it is among devas, nāgas, spirits, or any other such places, there is no offense.
"If a bhikṣu obtains a blade, he should destroy its characteristic as a weapon before using it."
If a bhikṣu sits upon a lump of gold or silver, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu touches gold or silver, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
*Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*, fascicle 2.
*Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*, Volume Three, translated by Saṃghavarman during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu bathes within the half-month period without an underlying cause and yet does not commit an offense? Answer: "There is. [In the case of] one who is..."
Regarding bathing in rain:
if a bhikṣu bathes while suffering from dizziness or exhaustion, there is no offense.
If he enters the water to lift a log and bathes as a consequence, there is no offense.
If one bathes in water due to some minor circumstance, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu bathes while learning to swim in order to cross water, there is no offense.
If, after the rainy season retreat has been entered for one month, one bathes repeatedly, there is no offense.
"After one month has passed, one should bathe every half-month.
If there is an intercalary month during the *varṣā* retreat, the days must be counted until they are complete.
"Is it possible for a bhikṣu to incur ten *pāyattikas* through a single means?"
Answer: "There is.
If one kills minute insects, one incurs a pāyattika offense for each one killed."
If one intends to cut a rattan vine but mistakenly cuts a snake, there is no offense.
If one intends to cut a snake but cuts a rattan vine, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one intends to kill this insect but kills that insect, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one intends to cut an insect but cuts the ground instead, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one intends to crush an insect but crushes the soil instead, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one sends a messenger by means of a hand signal to kill an insect, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one causes a person who is staying as a thief-monk (*cora-vāsika*), one who has originally violated the precepts, one who was originally not in harmony with the community, or one who is training under the precepts to feel doubt or regret, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
With the exception of monks and nuns, if one causes any other person to feel doubt or regret, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī to fall into doubt or regret, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī causes a bhikṣu to fall into doubt or regret, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī causes a śikṣamāṇā, or even a śrāmaṇerikā, to fall into doubt or regret, it is a duṣkṛta.
"Is there a case where a bhikṣu touches a bhikṣu’s body-organ and does not commit a pāyattika offense? Answer: "There is."
"If one touches another with a finger when their body-sense organ is impaired, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu pours a single vessel of water over various bhikṣus, he incurs as many *pāyattikas* as there are [drops] that adhere; for those that do not adhere, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu sits and drips water onto the ground, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣuṇī causes her own milk to flow, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu bathes and plays in water, splashing and submerging himself, it is a pāyattika.
If one plays by pouring ghee, oil, sugar, or honey over the body while bathing, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu stays overnight with a woman and does not commit a *pāyattika* offense?"
He replied: "There is.
That is to say, [committing it] against a wall, a tree, or within a large empty house constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense."
"With what kind of woman does one spend the night?
That is to say, with one whose body may be grasped.
If they share a connected dwelling, a common dining hall, or a single door, and spend the night together therein, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If one does not know that a person who has not yet received full ordination has entered to stay overnight, there is no offense.
"Is there a case where a bhikṣu causes fear in another bhikṣu and yet does not commit a pāyattika offense?"
Answer: "There are.

Namely: one who dwells as a thief, one who has originally transgressed the precepts, one who was originally not in harmony, one training in the precepts, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, and a śrāmaṇerī—[if they do so], it is a duṣkṛta."
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu conceals another bhikṣu’s robes, bowl, or other belongings without committing a pāyattika offense? Answer: "There is."
"Storing gold, silver, or alms bowls constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Using impure robes, an impure *niṣīdana*, a bowl bag, or similar items constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
How does one commit an offense regarding the five types of persons to whom one may give robes through a formal act of purification (*śuddhaka-dāna*)?
If more than ten nights have passed and the light of dawn appears, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu says:
"I saw such-and-such a person sitting or lying down together with such-and-such a woman."
[Pāyattika. To defame a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu knows they are a band of thieves and knows they are women, yet travels together with them on the road, it is a pāyattika.
If one returns by the middle path, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
"Is there a case where a bhikṣu traveling with thieves on the road does not commit a *pāyattika* offense? Answer:
"There is. It is not an offense if one travels together with those who have been led away by bandits, or on a dangerous road, or with yakṣas and others who steal the vital essence of humans.

If there is an invitation for four months—whether for the community or for an individual, whether for food, clothing, or other requisites—one may accept them; to accept more than that is a pāyattika."
If one repeatedly requests [what is needed], there is no offense.
If a lay donor (dānapati) invites a bhikṣu, saying:
"Whatever you require, simply come and take it."
After he had spoken these words, that bhikṣu left the monastic life; having received the full ordination again, he returned to the house of his original donor. Should he be invited once more?
He replied,
“You must request it again.
[The other asked,] “If the householder passes away, he will have other sons.”
"Must he be invited again? Is it by means of the previous method?
He replied, "He must be invited again."
“Householder, if a bhikṣu has previously been invited by you, but you have performed the *kapāla-āvṛti* (bowl-covering) *karmavācanā* against him, may he receive [the offering]?
He replied:
“He may not receive it; one who receives it commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.”
The householder said:
"If you do not accept it, I shall give rise to great disrespect and lack of faith.
Is it permissible for you to receive it?
Answer: "It is not permitted.
Only after causing him to repent and attain purification may you then receive it."
"If one has not yet reached twenty years of age, or if there is doubt regarding the age, and one confers the full ordination upon them, does he obtain the full ordination?
Answer: "He does not obtain it; the Saṃgha commits a duṣkṛta offense."

If a person receiving full ordination knows for themselves that they are less than twenty years of age, yet claims to be twenty at the time of ordination, there is no offense in performing communal acts with them.
However, if it is later discovered that this person is indeed less than twenty, the Sangha may not perform communal acts with them, because they did not originally obtain the precepts.
Regarding the four types of receiving the precepts according to their respective cases:
as for the "four types," they were originally not in harmony; as explained in the *Vibhaṅga-vinaya*, the subsequent performance of the *karmavācanā* was not accomplished.
What is meant by this?

One does not know for oneself that one is less than twenty years of age, yet later it is discovered that one is indeed less than twenty; having participated in the *poṣadha* and *karmavācanā* of the Saṃgha as one of the twelve members, this is called "living like a thief" (*caura-vāsa*).
"From what point are years and ages counted?
They are counted from the mother's womb, including all intercalary months.
If one digs up dead soil or disturbed earth, there is no offense, provided it is separated from its original nature.
What is "ground that has been prepared"?
That which has been left for four months during the summer is called ground that has been prepared.
To send a messenger or use hand-signs to have the ground dug constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one rises from one's seat and departs while the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is being made, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one rises and departs after the announcement has been made but before the formal ritual act (*karman*) has been performed, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one rises and departs during an illegal ritual act (*adharma-karman*), it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one performs a *karmavācanā* and departs together with those who reside as thieves, those who have originally violated the precepts, those who have originally been discordant, those training in the precepts (*śikṣamāṇā*), female probationers (*śikṣamāṇā*), male novices (*śrāmaṇera*), or female novices (*śrāmaṇerī*), it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one dispatches a person who has not yet completed his year of ordination (*anupasaṃpanna*) as a messenger, both parties incur a *duṣkṛta* offense.
When that person returns, [the sender] incurs a *pāyattika* and a *duṣkṛta*.
If one uses a wooden figure through incantations (*mantra*) as a messenger, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu acts as an advocate for others in a legal dispute, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
"If one cooks the 'timely medicine,' the 'non-timely medicine,' or the 'seven-day medicine' with alcohol, may it be consumed?"
"If there is no nature of alcohol, it may be consumed.
"May one eat all kinds of fruit-rice?
He replied:
"May you eat.
If a bhikṣu instructs a bhikṣuṇī in the Sūtra, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma, and says:
"I cannot study this."
If one goes to other bhikṣus and does not study anything except the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If a bhikṣu, whether on behalf of the Saṃgha or for his own private affairs, enters a village at three locations—namely, a layperson’s house, a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka), or the vicinity of a village—and does not announce his arrival, he commits no offense provided there is no other bhikṣu present. If there is no other bhikṣu present, he commits no offense even if he does not announce his arrival.
When various people dwell together, entering a village without having announced one's arrival does not constitute an offense.
"If one is on the ground and announces it to someone in the air, does this constitute a formal announcement?"
Answer: "The motion (jñapti) is established.
The same procedure is performed for the contrary case as well."
If one does not depart, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
When seeing a bhikṣu at a crossroads, one should announce [one's intention]; if not, once the thought has arisen, one should depart.
If one leaves the boundary within a single precinct and enters another place where there is no bhikṣu, one should announce [the matter] to a bhikṣuṇī; this applies likewise even to a śrāmaṇerikā.

Having accepted one invitation, he further accepts an impure offering; having eaten, he enters a village at his own pleasure without receiving the *śeṣa-bhakta* (leftover food) procedure. He commits two *pāyattika* offenses: for not receiving the *śeṣa-bhakta* and for entering the village without having announced himself.
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu enters the royal palace before the dawn has appeared and before the king has hidden his treasures, yet commits no offense? Answer: "There is."
If it is the residence of a king of devas, a nāga king, a yakṣa king, or any other non-human king,
and one enters because of an urgent cause or for the purpose of concealing treasure, there is no offense.
If, when the Prātimokṣa is being recited, a bhikṣuṇī says,
"I only now know of this offense," she commits a duṣkṛta.
When teaching other dharmas, excluding the Vinaya, if one says,
"I have only now learned that this dharma was taught during the half-month [of the rainy retreat]," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"Is there a case where a bhikṣu makes a bed-leg exceeding eight finger-breadths in height and yet does not commit a pāyattika offense?
Answer: "There is."
If one makes a bed using precious materials, such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, or crystal, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one makes one for another person and it exceeds eight finger-breadths [in height], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
“Is there any case where a bhikṣu sews a mat onto a sitting bed or a sleeping bed and does not commit an offense?
Answer: “There is.”
Except for cotton-filled mattresses, sewing other types of mattresses constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Sewing for another person constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Sending a messenger with a hand-seal constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To sew an impure mattress is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) and the *āvaraṇaka-vastra* (wound-covering cloth), one should understand them according to their respective cases.
To make a rain-cloak from an impure cloth is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one makes a robe out of impure cloth with measurements equal to those of a Sugata-robe, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The ninety *pāyattika* rules are concluded. 7.

Inquiry on the Four *Pratideśanīya* Rules: Regarding the four *pratideśanīya* rules, if one receives food from three types of persons in the house of a layperson, it is a *duṣkṛta*: namely, one who lives as a thief (*cora-vihārin*), one who was originally not in harmony (*apratisaṃhita-pūrva*), and one training in the precepts (*śikṣamāṇā*).
If a bhikṣu receives food from a bhikṣuṇī while in the air, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu receives food from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and does not commit an offense?"
He replied: "There is.
A bhikṣu is in the monastery, while a bhikṣuṇī is in the house of a layperson."
“Is there any case where a bhikṣu receives food from a bhikṣuṇī who is not his mother and yet does not commit an offense? Answer: “There is.”
That is to say:
if one receives [an invitation] at the house of a layperson from a non-relative bhikṣuṇī with her consent, there is no offense.
If it is by means of a hand signal, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson to beg for food, and a bhikṣuṇī therein says,
"Give food to this bhikṣu," and that bhikṣu receives the food, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If one receives food from within a single household belonging to different families, or receives it on behalf of another, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"Is there any case where receiving food from a non-relative bhikṣuṇī constitutes an offense of the four categories of precepts?"
He replied: "There is.

If one wraps food in a robe and takes both the robe and the food; if one speaks coarse and wicked words in front of a woman; if one touches her inner body; or if one sends a messenger with a hand-sign to say 'give me soup' or 'give me rice,' and the bhikṣu does not stop him—he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
"If one receives food at the threshold of a door, there is no offense.
Likewise, receiving it from among one's relatives, there is no offense.
"If, in a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka) that is a place of fear, one who is not ill receives food indoors, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
There is no offense in the case of illness.
One should say to that householder:
"There is an obstacle here."
Or, if the king asks the bhikṣu,
"Is there a thief in this place or not?
he replies:
"No. However, if there are thieves within this boundary, receiving food does not constitute an offense.
If one receives food outside the boundary, it does not constitute an offense.
If one sees a householder delivering food while on the middle path and says to them,
"Do not enter," yet the person enters of their own accord, there is no offense.
"If a bhikṣu is insane, he does not commit an offense.
Is there any case where a bhikṣu receives food with his own hand from a student's family and yet does not commit an offense? Answer:
“There is. That is, when one has been previously invited, or when one is ill.
The *pāṭidesanīya* rules are concluded.

8. The Seven Methods for Settling Disputes: Regarding the seven methods for settling disputes, if a bhikṣu commits an offense while insane and later remembers the transgression, it should be settled and eliminated according to the Dharma.
If he does not remember it, there is no offense.
If one wishes to raise a formal accusation (*adhikaraṇa*), one should first cause that bhikṣu to speak for himself, and only then raise the accusation.
First, one should request permission and seek out a *talaṭṭha* (an impartial mediator).
A *talaṭṭha* is one who has no partiality toward either of the two factions.
If they are not in agreement, one should not raise the matter; if one raises it, it is not called *talaṭṭha*.

One who acts as a *talaṭṭha* should know how to receive the voting sticks from both sides. If, having performed the act, one later says that it was not done, one incurs the offense of intentional lying.

Just as with "not being deluded," one should understand that "seeking out the offense" (mūlāpatti), "resolution in the presence of the accused" (sammukhavinaya), "resolution through confession" (pratijñāvinaya), "resolution through recollection" (smṛtivinaya), and "covering over with grass" (tṛṇaprastāraka) should be understood according to their respective meanings.
Upāli’s Questions on the Analysis of the Prātimokṣa are completed. 9.
Questions on the Matter of Receiving Ordination. Question:
"If one receives full ordination without performing the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, does one obtain full ordination or not?"
He replied, "No. [The questioner asked:
"If one abandons the preceptor at the time of receiving full ordination, does one obtain the full precepts or not?"
He replied, “One does not. [The questioner asked:

“When receiving the full precepts, if the officiant does not recite the three names—namely, the name of the preceptor, the name of the Sangha, and the name of the recipient—does one obtain the precepts or not?”
He replied:
"The precepts are not obtained.
[The Buddha said: "If, after the announcement (*jñapti*) has been made, the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is shortened, one obtains the precepts."
"Is it that one does not obtain the precepts?
"Answer: One does not obtain them.
When receiving the full precepts, one does not request an upādhyāya."
"Does one obtain the precepts or not?
He replied,
"One obtains the precepts."
“The assembly of monks has committed a *duṣkṛta* offense.
[Question: “When receiving full ordination, if one confers the precepts without first inquiring about the obstructing factors (*antarāyikadharma*), does the recipient obtain the precepts? Answer:
"He has received the precepts;
the bhikṣus have committed a duṣkṛta offense.
"If one grants full ordination to a foolish person, does he receive the precepts or not?"
Answer: "He obtains the precepts.
The bhikṣus commit a duṣkṛta offense."
“If two people undergo the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) together but receive the precepts at two different locations, do they obtain the precepts?
Answer: “They obtain the precepts.”
This refers to performing a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) between two boundaries.
"Is it possible for a bhikṣu to confer the precepts upon a person through a ritual performed with those from four locations, and thereby obtain the precepts?"
Answer: "One obtains the precepts.
That is to say, while sitting on a chair or a bed, one performs the *karmavācanā* facing the four directions."
"Is it possible for a bhikṣu to confer full ordination upon a person belonging to five categories and perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā), such that the recipient obtains the precepts?
Answer: "He obtains the precepts."
This refers to sitting on a chair or a bed while performing the *karmavācanā* for persons belonging to five groups:
eight persons, twelve persons, fifteen persons, and eighteen persons; it is the same for these as well.
“If a bhikṣu, while the community within the boundary is not in harmony, confers full ordination upon another, does that person obtain the precepts? Answer: “He does not.”
“What is meant by ‘defiling a bhikṣuṇī’? Answer:
“It refers to unchaste conduct; this is called defiling a bhikṣuṇī.”
“Does a person who defiles a bhikṣuṇī by means of eight matters constitute an act of defilement?
Answer: “It constitutes an act of defilement.”
“If eight people each defile a bhikṣuṇī by means of a single act, does this constitute defiling a bhikṣuṇī?
He replied:
“It does not constitute defiling a bhikṣuṇī.”
"What is meant by a 'thief-dweller' (corāvasika)? Answer:

"If one has not received full ordination through the formal procedure of *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, yet participates in the *jñapti-dvitīya* and *jñapti-caturtha* procedures, the *poṣadha*, and the *pravāraṇa*, and furthermore counts among the number of the twelve [monks], this is called a thief-dweller."
"If the person receiving the precepts does not know that the preceptor is a 'thief-dweller' (a false monk), and they rely on him to go forth and receive full ordination, do they obtain the precepts?
Answer: "They obtain the precepts."
"The various bhikṣus have committed duṣkṛta offenses.
The same applies to those who originally violated the precepts and those who were originally not in harmony.
"If a layperson serves as the upādhyāya and confers full ordination upon a layperson, does that person obtain the precepts?"
He replied:
"The precepts were obtained;
however, the bhikṣus have committed a duṣkṛta offense."
"If one who is not a renunciant acts as an upādhyāya and confers full ordination upon another, does that person obtain the precepts?
He replied,
"He obtains the precepts."
“What is meant by a person who has crossed over? Answer:

“It refers to one who discards the robes of a śramaṇa and abandons the precepts, goes to the abode of non-Buddhists, puts on their clothing, and takes pleasure in their views; such is a person who has crossed over.”
“Can one who has killed their mother be granted the going-forth and receive full ordination?
The answer is:
‘In some cases they may receive it; in other cases they may not.’”
How can one receive the full precepts?
If one intends to kill another mother but instead kills one's own mother, one may still be granted ordination and receive the full precepts.
However, if one intentionally takes the life of one's own mother, one cannot be granted ordination and receive the full precepts.
"Killing one's father or killing an Arhat is likewise.
Regarding the shedding of a Buddha’s blood with an evil mind, one may or may not be permitted to leave the household life and receive full ordination.
"How can one receive the full ordination after having left the household life? Answer:
"One who has not intentionally shed the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind may receive the full ordination after having left the household life."
Why is it that one does not incur [the offense]?
Because blood was drawn with an evil mind.
As for one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha, they may or may not be permitted to go forth and receive full ordination.
If one perceives the Dharma when receiving the voting tally (*śalākā*), and because of that perception the Saṃgha is split, one may be granted full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If one perceives it as non-Dharma, one may not be granted full ordination.
"If one confers full ordination upon a person of dull faculties, does he obtain the precepts?
Answer: "He obtains the precepts."
"Monks who commit a *duṣkṛta* offense [are as such];
the same applies to an impure person.
"If one confers full ordination upon a deaf person, does he obtain the precepts?"
He replied:
"If one hears the *karmavācanā*, one obtains the precepts; if one does not hear it, one does not obtain them.
It is the same for those who are deaf, those who are insane, those in the assembly whose minds are distracted, and those who are gravely ill."
If those who receive the precepts are not persons authorized to confer them, even if the number of such persons is complete, one does not obtain the precepts.
If those who receive the precepts are persons authorized to confer them, but the number of such persons is not complete, one does not obtain the precepts.

"If one who has been suspended for not seeing [an offense] confers the full ordination upon another person who has also been suspended for not seeing [an offense], does that person receive the precepts?
He replied:
"If that person says they see their offense, they receive the precepts."
The same applies to one who has not been expelled for holding evil and heterodox views.
If a monk who is part of the quorum for a formal act (*karmavācanā*) undergoes a change of gender after hearing the *karma*, he obtains the precepts.
"If a person who has received full ordination undergoes a change of gender, does he still possess full ordination?"
He replied, "The precepts have been received.
[The Buddha said: "As the Buddha has taught, a bhikṣuṇī must request the ordination from a bhikṣu."
"Therefore, if the preceptor changes their gender, do they obtain full ordination?
"If they change their gender after the *karmavācanā* has been heard, they obtain the full precepts.
"If the person receiving the precepts is on the ground while the *karmavācanā* is performed in the air, do they obtain the precepts?"
Answer: "It is not permitted.
The same applies to the opposite case as well."
"How does one obtain the full precepts?
If it is through the formal procedure of the motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), this is called obtaining the precepts.
Thus ends the inquiry regarding the matter of receiving the precepts.

10. Questions on the Matters of the Poṣadha. Regarding the demarcation of the boundary for a village (*grāma-sīmā*): one must exclude the village and its boundary, and then demarcate the boundary for not being separated from one's robes (*acīvara-vippavāsa-sīmā*), because the village and its boundary do not constitute the robe-boundary.
If the assembly is seated on the ground while the boundary is established in the air, the boundary is not successfully established.
The same applies to the opposite case.
If they are in an *āraṇyaka* (forest hermitage), the boundary should face one *krośa*; within that space, there shall be a single *poṣadha*.
If one faces a distance of one *krośa* and does not see a bhikṣu within it, how can the *poṣadha* be performed?
If one performs the *poṣadha* together with others within the range of one's vision, one must likewise generate the formal intention (*cittotpāda*).
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"If a bhikṣu is on the ground and one who has given their consent (chanda) is in the air, does the giving of the purity-authorization (pārisuddhi-chanda) become valid?
Answer: "It does not become valid."
"If one has received the pure consent (*śuddhaka-rocana*), one loses that pure consent immediately upon going outside the boundary.
Is there a case where a bhikṣu recites the Prātimokṣa in two places and the recitation is considered valid?"
He replied:
"It is established as being said that this refers to the interval between two realms. [The questioner asked:
"Is it possible for a bhikṣu to give the *śuddhaka-icchā* (the desire for purity) in three places and perform the *poṣadha* in three places, and yet have the giving of the *śuddhaka-icchā* be valid?"
Answer: "It can be accomplished;
that is, when one is in the intermediate state between realms."
“If a madman recites the *poṣadha*, is the recitation of the *poṣadha* accomplished?
Answer: “The recitation of the *poṣadha* is accomplished.”
“When a resident bhikṣu expels another bhikṣu during the uposatha, if a visiting bhikṣu arrives, may he perform the *karmavācanā* together with them?
Answer: “If the *karmavācanā* is performed in accordance with the Dharma, he may perform it together with them.”
What constitutes rising from the assembly?
If a single bhikṣu rises to attend to the needs of nature (for defecation or urination) without leaving the range of hearing, it is not called rising from the assembly.
If he leaves the range of hearing, this is called rising from the assembly.
"If a deaf person recites the *Poṣadha* in a full assembly, the recitation of the *Poṣadha* is considered accomplished.
The same applies to people from border regions or those who are dull-witted and slow.
"If the Saṃgha is split at the time of the *Poṣadha*, how should the monks perform the *Poṣadha*?"
He replied, “Each speaks the precepts within their own respective factions. [The Buddha asked:
“Is it possible for bhikṣus sitting in four separate locations to perform the recitation of the precepts and thereby fulfill the requirements of the saṃgha?”
Answer: "The recitation of the precepts is accomplished.
This refers to whether one is on a sitting bench or a bed."
The inquiry regarding the *poṣadha* ceremony is concluded. 11.
Inquiry regarding the *pravāraṇā* ritual: If the *pravāraṇā* is performed on the ground together with those in the air, the *pravāraṇā* is not validly accomplished.
The same applies to the opposite case.
"Is there a case where a bhikṣu performs the *pravāraṇā* at two locations and it is considered a valid *pravāraṇā*?
Answer: "There is."
"This refers to being in the intermediate state between two realms;
the same applies to the four places of self-indulgence.
As the Buddha has taught, one's offenses are cleared when there is purity and a shared vision."
"How is it that those who are pure see the same thing?
'Seeing the same thing' refers to the Prātimokṣa.
"As it has been said, if there arises another difficulty besides the dangers of water or fire, may one perform the *pravāraṇā* with a single utterance?"
Answer: "If each individual difficulty arises, one may perform the *pravāraṇā* with a single statement for each.

As the Buddha has taught, once these matters are excluded, one performs the *pravāraṇā* regarding other matters; that is to say, having excluded the persons, one performs the *pravāraṇā* regarding other matters.
What is the matter?
Who is the person?
If the offense was committed by that person, then exclude that person.
As the Buddha has taught, when the time for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) arrives, the offenses of the bhikṣus are brought forth.

Some say they have committed a *pāyattika*, some say they have committed a *pratideśanīya*, some say they have committed an offense requiring mental regret (*cittavipratisāra*), and some say they have committed a *duṣkṛta*.
What is the matter?
It refers to the *pāṭidesanīya* (offenses requiring confession).

If the resident saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day, and many guest monks arrive, they perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fourteenth day; the resident bhikṣus should go outside the boundary to perform their *pravāraṇā*.
"As the Buddha has taught, one should go outside the boundary for the *pravāraṇā*.
Should all the bhikṣus go outside the boundary together, or should each individual go outside? Answer:
"Everyone shall perform the *pravāraṇā* outside the boundary.
[Question: "Once the *pravāraṇā* has been performed, may one who has been expelled (*pārājika*) live together with the community? Answer:
"No. How does one become separated from the community?
As previously explained.

If a community is full of deaf people, or full of foolish people, or full of people from border regions, or full of bhikṣus who have not received the Dharma, the number is insufficient for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony to be valid.
If the person performing the *pravāraṇā* changes their gender, the *pravāraṇā* is not accomplished.
The inquiry regarding the matter of *pravāraṇā* is concluded. 12.
Inquiry on the Rules for the Rains Retreat (*varṣā*) Inquiry on the Rules for the Rains Retreat: "If a monk, during the rains retreat, expels another monk, may they dwell together?"
He replied:
"One may dwell together for three months. [The questioner asked:
"If a bhikṣu dwells in the open air during the rains retreat, and the dawn appears, does he lose his rains retreat?"
He replied: "The *anvāsaṃvāsa* (the formal residence for the rains retreat) has been lost.
[The Buddha said: "If the Saṃgha has already entered the rains retreat within a village and departs beyond its boundary, and other bhikṣus subsequently establish a new boundary there."
"In this case, when a donor gives robes to the community of monks, to whom do these robes belong?
Answer: "They belong to the community of monks of the previous village."
"As the Buddha has taught, this is the benefit of the merit of the *dhātu*.
If the Saṃgha is split during the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), to which group of monks should this gift of robes belong? Answer:
"As for those who belong to many [monasteries], there are four reliances:
namely, reliance on the summer retreat, reliance on the time, reliance on food, and reliance on the *pravāraṇā*.
Is it possible for a bhikṣu to perform the summer retreat in four places and perform the *pravāraṇā* in four places?"
He replied:
"There is. If one sits or lies down upon a bed."
The inquiry regarding the rules for the rainy season retreat (varṣā) is concluded.
13. Inquiry regarding the rules for medicine: "If a lifetime medicine is kept on impure ground, may it be eaten after having spent the night there?"
He replied,
"I may not. [The Buddha asked,] "May one eat human milk?"
Answer: “It is not permitted.
However, it is permitted to apply it to other parts of the body.”
"If impure oil mixed with salt is boiled, may it be eaten?
He replied, "It may."
"It means it is diseased, not undiseased.
Flesh is also like this.
"If fire is on impure ground and a person on pure ground performs the ritual of purification (kappiya-kāraṇa), may one eat it?"
He replied, “One may eat it. [The questioner asked:
“If fire is on impure ground and the meat is near the edge of the fire, and no one has performed the ritual purification (*kappiya-karaṇa*), does it become pure?”
"May I eat it?
He replied, "It has been rendered pure; you may eat it."
“As the Buddha has taught, one must not consume the fat of insects.
May it be used for other purposes?
He replied:
"One may not eat it, but it may be used for other purposes.
"If fire is on impure ground and a pure person is on pure ground, is the clarified butter (sarpis) pure and fit to be eaten?"
He replied, “One may eat it. [The questioner asked:
“Aside from the eight kinds of fermented drinks, if one makes a drink from other substances, may it be drunk?”
He replied,
"If it is clear and pure, it may be drunk.
Thus ends the inquiry regarding medicinal matters.
14. Inquiry on the Rules for Robes. Regarding the rules for robes: "A bhikṣu who has been expelled during the rainy season retreat does not receive the summer robe-cloth.
Is there any case where a bhikṣu may beg for a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative without committing an offense?"
He replied: "There is.
If one begs for a robe for a cell, or begs on behalf of the Saṃgha, or if a person training in the precepts begs, or if one sends a messenger to beg for a robe."
It is a *dukkaṭa*.
How is a robe obtained?
If it is on one's knees or in one's hands, or if it is on one's shoulder, this is called obtaining a robe.
"If one begs for a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative and does not obtain it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"If a bhikṣu takes a robe from four places, is there no offense?"
He replied:
"There is. If one is sitting or lying upon a bed."
The inquiry regarding robes is concluded. 15.

Inquiry on the Method for Receiving the Kaṭhina Cloth: "If one has already performed the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to criticism) in another location and then arrives at yet another location, is it permissible to receive the kaṭhina cloth?"
Answer: "One may accept it;
however, one may not dwell [in the monastery], and the benefit of the robe will be reduced in measure."
"If one undergoes the formal acceptance (*saṃvṛti*) by making a *kaṭhina* robe, is the acceptance valid?
He replied:
"The acceptance is not valid."
“As the Buddha has taught, regarding the matters permitted for a bhikṣu who has received the kaṭhina robe: does this constitute a relinquishing of the precepts, or is it an opening of permission?
Answer: “It is an opening of permission; it is not a relinquishing of the precepts.”
“If a bhikkhu, during the rains retreat, demarcates a cattle-pen as the inner boundary and then relinquishes it after the *pravāraṇā*,
to whom does a robe offered by a donor therein belong?”
He replied:
"It belongs to those who previously entered the rains retreat.
As the Buddha has taught, this is the benefit of the rains retreat."
"Is there a case where a monk accepts a single robe as the kaṭhina-cloth, yet that very acceptance is not valid?
Answer: "There is."
That is to say, there are those who rely on the intercalary month and those who do not.

Among them, those who rely on the intercalary month perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony after the *varṣā* retreat; if they obtain robes on the ninth day, they may accept them and perform the *kaṭhina* ceremony.
For those who do not rely on the intercalary month, the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* is valid; for those who do rely on it, the acceptance is not valid.

When the king establishes an intercalary month, once the days of the rainy season retreat (vassa) have been counted to completion and the invitation ceremony (pravāraṇā) has been performed, the acceptance of the kaṭhina robe is valid; at the time of the uposatha, the kaṭhina robe is relinquished.
If the Saṃgha is split during the rainy season retreat, those who act in accordance with the Dharma should accept the kaṭhina robe.
If both sides accept the kaṭhina robe, those who act in accordance with the Dharma shall obtain the benefits of their residence.
When receiving the kaṭhina robe, how does one express approval?
By expressing approval in person.
How does one hear of the relinquishing of the kaṭhina?
If one goes outside the boundary and hears from another that the *kaṭhina* robe has been relinquished,
how is the robe lost?
It means the robe that was being made is lost.
What constitutes a "finished robe"?
It is when the robe that was being made has been completed.
Thus it is explained in detail.
If a bhikṣu who abides in his original status (prakṛtistha) receives the kaṭhina robe, who should express their approval?
It is said that both the bhikṣu who abides in his original status and the suspended bhikṣu (pravāsanīya) should do so.
If the suspended bhikṣu expresses their approval, it likewise constitutes the formal acceptance of the kaṭhina.
The questions concerning the *kaṭhina* robe are concluded. 16.

Questions concerning the matter of Kauśāmbī. Regarding the matter of Kauśāmbī: "If a formal act (*karmavācanā*) of banishment is performed against a bhikṣu, and the one being banished is asleep, is the banishment valid?"
He replied:
"If one hears the formal announcement (*jñapti*), the expulsion is accomplished. [The questioner asked:
"If the full assembly of bhikṣus is asleep, is the expulsion accomplished?"
“If one hears the proclamation, is the formal act of banishment accomplished?
“If, while the formal act (kamma) is being performed for a monk who has been banished, many monks hear it, is the banishment accomplished by two persons?”
He replied:
"Even if only one person hears it, the act of banishment is accomplished.
[The questioner asked: "If the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī each form two factions, does this constitute a schism in the Saṃgha, or not?"
He replied:
"It is not a schism in the Saṃgha. Why is that?"
It is not because of performing a formal act (*karmavācanā*) based on the thought that the Sangha is being split.
When the Bhikṣus of Vaiśālī raised ten points, the elder Bhikṣus neither supported this side nor that side; they were called *tāla-vṛtta* (palm-tree-like) Bhikṣus.
The inquiry concerning the matter of Kauśāmbī is concluded. 17.
Inquiry Concerning the Matter of Karma. Regarding the matter of karma: "If a deaf person fulfills the required number for performing a *karmavācanā*, is the performance of the karma valid?"
Answer: "If they hear it, the *karmavācanā* is accomplished.
This is likewise for those who are dull-witted and for those from border regions."
If a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed by monks who have received the Dharma, but the full quorum is made up by monks who have not received the Dharma, the *karmavācanā* is not valid.
If a *karmavācanā* is performed while some persons are on the ground and others are in the air, it is not validly performed.
"Inconsistency is also like this. [Question:
"Is it possible for a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) performed in two places to be considered successfully accomplished? Answer:
"It is accomplished;
that is to say, within the boundary.
"Is it possible for four places to perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) for four persons such that it is accomplished?"
Answer: "It constitutes an act.

That is to say, if one prepares a seat or a bed, such as for performing a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), a *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), or a *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) against a bhikṣu."
If one performs [a ritual] for a śrāmaṇera in such a manner, it does not constitute a valid performance.
If the śrāmaṇera is on the ground while the [performing monks] are in the air, the karmavācanā is not valid.
The same applies to cases of discordance.
“Is it possible for a single formal act (*karmavācanā*) to expel four śrāmaṇeras, and for that expulsion to be valid?
He replied: “It is.”
"It means being within the boundaries.
"Is it possible that by expelling four śrāmaṇeras at four separate locations, the expulsion is accomplished? Answer:
“There are. Namely, sitting beds and reclining beds.
Thus ends the inquiry regarding the *karmavastu*.

18. Inquiry on the Concealment of Saṃghāvaśeṣa Offenses. Inquiry on the Concealment of Saṃghāvaśeṣa Offenses: "Is there any bhikṣu who, having committed one of the thirteen matters, does not confess it for the rest of his life and yet remains unoffended?"
Answer: "There is.
That is to say, if during the day one is in a place where there is a bhikṣu, but at night one is in a place where there is no bhikṣu, it does not constitute concealment."
If one confesses to a deaf person, it constitutes a confession, yet one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It is the same when confessing to a foolish person or a person from a frontier region.
Likewise, if one confesses to someone who has received the Dharma or someone who has not received the Dharma;
"If one does not receive [the confession] from a legal person (*pudgala*), but confesses before one who has received it, in all such cases the confession is valid.
[Question: "Before whom must one conceal [a fault] for it to constitute concealment? Answer:
"If one does not confess before a bhikṣu who possesses the nature [of being a proper recipient], from that point it is called 'concealment.
What is concealed by a deaf person is not called concealment.
What is concealed by a foolish person or by a person from a border region is not called concealment."
"If a person is on the ground while another is in the air, it is not called 'concealment.
The same applies to the opposite case.
Is there a case where a bhikṣu confesses in two places and thereby achieves confession?"
Answer: "There is.
It refers to the interval between the two realms."
If a *dharmika* bhikṣu conceals [an offense] from a non-*dharmika* bhikṣu, it does not constitute concealment.
The same applies to the opposite case.

Concealing [an offense] from a bhikṣu who has been suspended (*pravāsanīya*), from one who is undergoing the *parivāsa* probation, from one who has completed the *parivāsa*, from one who is undergoing the *mānatva* penance, from one who has completed the *mānatva*, from one who is insane, from one who is deranged, from one who is suffering from illness, or from a layperson (*avadātavasana*)—in all these cases, it is not termed concealment.
“Is it possible for a bhikṣu who has attained the four bases [of power] and four bhikṣus to perform an *ābhāhana*? Answer: “It is.”
That is to say, while sitting or lying upon a bed.
From what location is one granted the *parivāsa* (probation)?
That is to say, from wherever there are bhikṣus within the boundary (*sīmā*).
“Is there any bhikṣu who, throughout his life, conceals a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense without confessing it, yet does not thereby commit an offense?
Answer: “There is.”
This refers to one who has originally committed a *pārājika* offense.
The inquiry concerning the concealment of offenses is concluded. 19.
Inquiry Concerning the Suspension of the *Poṣadha*: Regarding the suspension of the *poṣadha*, as the Buddha has taught, it concerns the suspension of a bhikṣu from the *poṣadha*.
When is it a valid prohibition?
It is at the time of the *poṣadha*, not at a time when the *poṣadha* is not being held.
To prohibit the *poṣadha* using the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) does not constitute a valid prohibition; one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Having heard [the announcement] with the divine ear, if one prohibits the *poṣadha*, or if a deaf person prohibits the *poṣadha*, the prohibition is not valid.

Whether it be a foolish person, a person from a border region, one who has received the Dharma, or one who has not received the Dharma—whether on the ground or in the air—all such prohibitions are invalid; one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"Is it possible for a bhikṣu to perform the recitation of the precepts in two places and yet have the recitation successfully accomplished?
Answer: "The recitation of the precepts is successfully accomplished."
"It refers to the intermediate space between the two realms.
"Is it possible for four bhikṣus to perform a single recitation of the *poṣadha* at four locations? Answer:
“There is. If one is seated on a chair or lying on a bed, it is obstructed.
The same applies to the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; this is explained in detail.”
The inquiry concerning the matter of the *poṣadha* suspension is concluded. 20.

Inquiry Concerning the Matter of Bedding and Furniture Regarding the matter of bedding and furniture: "If two bhikṣus request bedding and furniture, the senior (*sthavira*) should be the first to use it; once he has finished using it, he should give it to the second bhikṣu."
"Is it permissible to sit together with one who has not yet received full ordination on a mat spread upon the ground?
He replied,
"It is permissible to sit together."
“As the Buddha has taught, an incoming bhikṣu should perform his duties according to the Dharma and should pay homage to the senior bhikṣus.
If there is someone among them who is undergoing a separate residence (parivāsa), should he be paid homage?”
Answer: "One must not pay homage.
A visiting bhikṣu should not pay homage to two kinds of persons: namely, those undergoing parivāsa (probation) and those of lower standing."
The inquiry concerning bedding and requisites is concluded. 21.
Inquiry Concerning the Settling of Disputes: "If there is a dispute among bhikṣus, a bhikṣuṇī may not settle it; a dispute among bhikṣus must be settled by bhikṣus."
"Regarding disputes among bhikṣuṇīs, even up to disputes among śrāmaṇerikās, a bhikṣu settles them.

Just as with the *parivāsa* (probation), once the *parivāsa* is completed, one undergoes the *mānatva* (penance); once the *mānatva* is completed, one should sit below the bhikṣus. Should the bedding and seating also be given to those of lower status?"
He replied:
"Not so. It should be given in due order."
"First, one should provide bedding and requisites to those who have not yet reached their seniority, and only then to those who act contrary to the Dharma.
If an expelled person has extra bedding and requisites, these should be given to them.
"How does one settle a dispute?"
"If the Saṃgha settles a dispute by receiving voting tallies in accordance with the Dharma, it is so;
however, if the settling occurs by receiving tallies without those present, it is not called 'settling a dispute.
The inquiry concerning the matter of settling disputes is concluded.

22. Inquiry on the Matter of Schism in the Saṃgha. Regarding the matter of schism in the Saṃgha as taught by the Buddha: a schism in the Saṃgha occurs due to two causes and conditions, namely, hearing [the proposal] and receiving the voting tally; there is no third cause and condition for a schism in the Saṃgha.
If one who has been expelled is the ninth person [in the assembly], it is not called "schism.
The same applies to one who dwells as a thief (a *steyāśaya*) or one who possesses both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*).
The inquiry concerning the matter of schism is concluded.

23. Inquiry on the Matter of Covering the Alms Bowl (Pātra-Praticchādana). Regarding the matter of covering the bowl: when a householder has fulfilled two conditions, the formal act of *pātra-praticchādana* (covering the bowl) should be performed against them.
What are these two? They are:
reviling a bhikṣu and falsely accusing a pure bhikṣu with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense.
"Is there a case where a bhikṣu’s bowl is turned down by a householder in two places, thereby constituting a 'turned-down bowl'?
He replied: "There is."
That is to say, in the interval between two realms:
if a bhikṣu who upholds the Dharma turns over his alms-bowl (*pātra*) at the house of a donor who does not uphold the Dharma, the overturning of the bowl is not accomplished.
If a bhikṣu who has been expelled turns over his alms-bowl at the house of a donor who dwells in his original nature, the overturning of the bowl is not accomplished.
"It is the same for one who lives as a thief.
"Is there a case where a bhikṣu, by means of four grounds, effects the bowl-covering (pātrabandhana) for four lay devotees (upāsaka), such that the bowl-covering is successfully accomplished? Answer:
"It is accomplished;
that is, on a chair or a couch.
If one confesses before a person who has previously committed an offense against the precepts, one commits a *duṣkṛta*."
To confess before one who lives as a thief, one who was originally not in harmony with the community, one training in the precepts, or a śrāmaṇera constitutes an offense of *duṣkṛta*.
It is the same when confessing before an expelled (*pravāsanīya*) bhikṣu.
The questions posed by Upāli were thus concluded. 24.

Miscellaneous Matters from the Vinayamātṛkā. Regarding the miscellaneous matters in the *Vinayamātṛkā*: The Buddha was staying at the Markaṭahradaka Hall in Vaiśālī and established a precept for Sūdanī, the son of Kalandaka.
At that time, Sudinna was filled with sorrow, anxiety, doubt, and remorse, and he thought to himself:
"The Buddha has said:
'Except for those who have previously committed an offense, there is no transgression.'"
"Before I had established the precepts, I engaged in many acts of sexual misconduct; I do not know which of these was committed first without constituting an offense.
The bhikṣus related this in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“You should know this: when I had not yet established the precepts, Sūtiputra committed an offense; at all other times, he did not commit an offense.
The bhikṣu Vajjiputta, without renouncing the precepts and without declaring his weakness in observing them, changed his robes and engaged in sexual misconduct.
Having committed sexual misconduct, he spoke these words:
"I shall question the bhikṣus; if I am permitted to go forth again, I shall do so;
if I am not permitted to go forth, I shall remain here."
He related these matters in detail to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus related them in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu has abandoned the precepts, or having left the order, has become weak in his vows, and then changes his robes and commits sexual misconduct, this person may again leave the household life and receive full ordination."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

If a bhikṣu, without having renounced the precepts and without his precepts being weakened or his intention to leave having been expressed, commits the act of sexual intercourse, that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense and shall not live in community with the others.
There was a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya. Not far from him, a female elephant gave birth to a female calf.
When the mother elephant went out to forage for food, the female calf came near the bhikṣu.

The bhikṣu gave her grass to eat and water to drink; as the female elephant crouched down to eat, her female organ was exposed. Upon seeing this, the bhikṣu conceived a mind of lustful attachment and engaged in sexual intercourse with her.
He immediately felt shame, remorse, doubt, and regret, thinking,
"I have committed a pārājika offense.
He related this in detail to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus related it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Because he did not touch the [actual] organ, he does not commit a *pārājika* offense, but commits a *sthūlātyaya* (thullaccaya) offense.

As that female elephant gradually grew up, her organ opened and became visible again. This bhikṣu again gave rise to a mind of lustful attachment; with his hand, he pressed against the female elephant's organ, intending to engage in sexual intercourse, whereupon the female elephant kicked the bhikṣu with her foot.
He immediately felt shame, remorse, and fear, and a sense of doubt and regret arose in his mind:
"I have committed a *pārājika* offense.
Because of this matter, he explained it in detail to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus explained it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"If one possesses a sense of fear and shame, one does not commit a pārājika offense, but commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
"As the Buddha has taught, one who is insane does not commit an offense."
"What constitutes madness?
He replied:

"There are five causes and conditions that are called madness: namely, the loss of kin, the loss of wealth, the disharmony of the four great elements, being afflicted by non-human spirits, and the retribution of past karma; these are known as the five kinds of madness."
"If he commits an act of transgression against the precepts, he incurs an offense according to the nature of the act if he knows himself to be a bhikṣu; if he does not know it, he incurs no offense.
"As the Buddha has taught, one with a distracted mind incurs no offense."
"What is a distracted mind? He replied:

"A distracted mind has five causes and conditions: namely, being terrified by non-human beings (amanuṣya), being struck by non-human beings, having one's vital energy (ojas) stolen by non-human beings, the disharmony of the four great elements (mahābhūta), and the retribution of past karma. These are called the five causes and conditions for a distracted mind."
"Violating the precepts is as previously explained.
"As the Buddha has taught, one who is in pain does not commit an offense.
What constitutes being in pain?"
He replied:

"There are five causes and conditions that are called painful sensations: namely, those arising from wind, those arising from cold, those arising from heat, those arising from their combination, and those arising from the seasons; these are called the five causes and conditions of painful sensation."
"The offense is as previously explained.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse while perceiving what is not the path as being the path,
he immediately gives rise to doubt and regret:
"I have committed a *pārājika* offense," he said, explaining it in detail to the bhikṣus. The bhikṣus explained it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If one perceives a path as a path, one commits a *pārājika* offense.
If one perceives a path as a non-path, one commits a *pārājika* offense.
If one perceives a non-path as a path, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense."
The three paths are the anus, the urethra, and the mouth.
If a bhikṣu [penetrates] the anus beyond the skin, it is a pārājika offense.
If he [penetrates] the urethra beyond the joint, it is a pārājika offense.
"If the mouth passes over the teeth, it is a *pārājika* offense.

This applies to monkeys, lions, badgers, peacocks, and chickens; as for those with naturally long penises, the full explanation is as given in the *Vinaya*, and all such cases constitute a *pārājika* offense.
The training rules for the bhikṣu Nanda are explained at length in the Vinaya.

If a bhikṣu bathes naked in the air while four other bhikṣus rub and massage his body, and through that mutual physical contact he gives rise to a defiled mind, taking the male organ of a bhikṣu and placing it in his mouth, only to spit it out immediately.
He then gave rise to doubt and regret, thinking,
"Have I committed a pārājika offense?
and he related this in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One does not commit a pārājika offense.
However, one must not bathe in the open air while having the body scrubbed or massaged; the same applies to sitting or lying down."
If a bhikṣu, with lust raging intensely, goes to a bhikṣu he loves and says,
"My lust is raging intensely," and that one replies:
"Go and commit sexual misconduct.
He then went and committed sexual misconduct.
That bhikṣu immediately gave rise to doubt and regret:
“If I instruct a bhikṣu to engage in sexual intercourse, do I incur a pārājika offense?
The Buddha said, “You do not incur a pārājika; you incur a sthūlātyaya.”
The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
how does one repent for a sthūlātyaya offense?"
The Buddha said to Upāli: “There are four types of *sthūlātyaya*:

namely, the grave *sthūlātyaya* bordering on a *pārājika*, the light *sthūlātyaya* bordering on a *pārājika*, the grave *sthūlātyaya* bordering on a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and the light *sthūlātyaya* bordering on a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.”
Regarding those offenses bordering on *pārājika* that are grave, one must confess before the entire assembly within the boundary;
those that are light, one confesses before four persons outside the boundary.
Regarding *saṃghāvaśeṣa* bordering on *sthūlātyaya*, one confesses before four persons outside the boundary.
"For minor offenses, one person shall perform confession.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who did not cover his mouth when yawning; another bhikṣu, whose lustful desire was intense, inserted his male organ into that bhikṣu’s mouth.
He immediately spat it out and was struck with doubt and regret, thinking:
"Have I committed a *pārājika* offense? ...
[and so on] ... until the Buddha said:
"One does not commit a *pārājika* offense.
From this day forward, one must cover the mouth when yawning; if one does not cover it, one commits a *dukkaṭa* offense.
There was a bhikṣu whose male organ was constantly erect, and he had this thought:
"It is not an offense to enter the female organ," he thought,
and he inserted it into the female organ.
He immediately felt doubt and regret.
"Have I committed a pārājika offense?
... until the Buddha said:
"Upon entering, one commits a pārājika offense."
A certain bhikṣu conceived a defiled mind toward his mother and said to her,
"I wish to engage in sexual intercourse.
His mother said to her son:
"Regarding the place from which you have emerged, act according to your will.
He then desired to engage in sexual intercourse, but upon reaching the female organ, he immediately felt shame and remorse.
He gave rise to a mind of regret:
"Have I committed a *pārājika* offense? ...
[and so on] until the Buddha said:
"If, at the time of feeling shame, one does not give rise to a lustful mind, one does not commit a *pārājika*; one commits a *sthūlātyaya*."
There was a bhikṣu who, while observing corpses in a wilderness, saw the corpse of a woman adorned with fine clothing; he conceived a defiled mind.
Grasping her female organ with his hand, he intended to enter it, but found that its interior was filled with worms. He immediately felt doubt and regret, thinking:
"Have I committed a pārājika offense?"
The Buddha continued, saying:
"There are two kinds of destruction, namely internal destruction and external destruction; in such cases, one does not commit a pārājika offense, but commits a sthūlātyaya offense."
There was a female lay follower named Suprabhā who passed away as the sun was setting.
Her kinsmen, having adorned her body, cast it into the wilderness.
A certain bhikṣu was there observing a corpse; upon seeing it, a defiled mind arose within him, and he seized the female organ, intending to enter it.
The corpse immediately sat up, and the bhikṣu gave rise to a mind of fear, doubt, and remorse, thinking:
"Have I committed a pārājika offense?
... until the Buddha said:
"In times of fear, there is no greed; one does not commit a *pārājika* offense, but commits a *sthūlātyaya*.
There was a laywoman named Sujātā.
A certain bhikṣu would enter and leave her house, and he said to that laywoman:
"I am bound by lust. He replied,
"If one employs a means below to bring it out above, or employs a means above to bring it out below, do we not experience pleasure therein?"
The bhikṣu then rebuked and reviled him,
saying, "You are a fool and a liar.
Having spoken these words, he nevertheless continued to carry out his duties with him.
The Buddha further said:
"To enter [the house] constitutes an offense of *pārājika*.
There was a householder’s wife; a bhikṣu would go in and out of her home and say to that woman:
“I am bound by lust.
His wife replied,
“Employ the expedient means as previously described.”
...and so on, until the Buddha said:
"To enter [the womb] constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
The circumstances concerning the bhikṣu Sundarananda are explained in detail in the Vinaya.
He lived alone in a forest hermitage, not far from a brahmin’s field.
That brahmin would frequently go to his field to inspect it, and upon seeing this bhikṣu, he felt a heart of joy; he immediately invited him for a meal, and the bhikṣu accepted the invitation.
After the brahmin had prepared various foods and drinks, he sent a naked young girl to the bhikṣu’s location to summon him.
Upon seeing the girl’s genitals, the bhikṣu gave rise to a defiled mind and engaged in sexual intercourse with her.
Her female organ was ruptured, and she immediately felt doubt and regret.
The Buddha then said:
