"If one experiences pleasure, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense; if one does not experience pleasure, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense."
There was a bhikṣu whose male organ never became erect, and he thought to himself:
"If one who has an erection commits sexual intercourse, he commits a pārājika offense; if one does not have an erection, there is no offense."
He then committed the act of sexual intercourse.
Thereupon the Buddha said:
"He does not commit a *pārājika* offense, but commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense."
There was a bhikṣu who was sleeping when a woman came to him and committed sexual intercourse; he then became doubtful and regretful.
Up to this point, the Buddha said:
"If she takes his hand with her hand, or his foot with her foot, or her thigh touches his thigh, it is a pārājika offense."
"If there is no contact, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
As it is with sleep, so it is with madness and delusion.
The four cases regarding women apply likewise to men and those who are neither male nor female.
There was a bhikṣu who, while asleep, was approached by a woman for sexual intercourse; that bhikṣu became doubtful and remorseful.
Eventually, the Buddha spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:
"Did you know [it was happening]?"
He replied, “I do not know.
I was awakened by movement.”
“If one is aware of the movement [of the organ], one does not commit a *pārājika* offense, but commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
A bhikṣu was asleep when a woman approached him and engaged in sexual intercourse; he immediately felt doubt and regret.
乃至佛言：「比丘！汝知不受樂不？」 Even unto the Buddha’s words: “Bhikṣu!
Do you know that you do not experience pleasure?”
He replied, “I did not experience pleasure. [The Buddha said:
“If you did not experience pleasure, there is no offense.”
There was a bhikṣu who, while asleep, was approached by a woman and engaged in sexual intercourse; he immediately felt doubt and regret. ...
[The matter] came before the Buddha, who said:
"Did you know that you were not experiencing pleasure?"
He replied, “I do not know.
I am aware of movement without experiencing pleasure.”
The Buddha said:
"He commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
As it is for a bhikṣu, so it is for a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, and a śrāmaṇerikā.
There was a wicked śrāmaṇera who said to a woman,
"If one enters all paths, there is no offense.
She then engaged in all such acts with him, whereupon she immediately gave rise to doubt and regret.
乃至佛言：「入即波羅夷。」如女人，男子亦如是。 The Buddha further said:
"If it enters, it is an *pārājika* offense.
As it is with a woman, so it is with a man.
There was a bhikṣu who, while asleep, was approached by a woman for sexual intercourse; he became doubtful and remorseful.
... [The matter] was brought before the Buddha, who said: "Did you know it?"
He replied, “I do not know.
“If you did not know, there is no offense.”
"Just as it is with a woman, so it is for a man who is not a male.
An evil bhikṣu says to a śikṣamāṇā:
'Since you have not yet received full ordination, committing sexual misconduct with me does not constitute an offense.'"
He consented immediately; having consented, he felt regret.
The bhikṣu forcibly seized him and committed sexual intercourse.
He was then filled with doubt and remorse:

"I have taken a *pāṃsukūla* robe," he thought, and immediately felt doubt and regret. ...
[The Buddha] spoke thus:
“There is no offense;
you should take it only after careful inspection.
A householder heard that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, would pick up any garment that had fallen on the ground and take it away.
The householder wrapped the eight *kāliṅga* robes inside his garment and buried them in a heap of refuse, leaving only a small portion visible before departing.
When a bhikṣu seeking discarded rags (*pāṃsukūla*) arrived at that place, he saw them and took them.
The householder said to the bhikṣu,
"Venerable sir!
Do not take my robe."
The bhikṣu said,
"I obtained it from among the discarded rags.
The householder replied to the bhikṣu:
"I heard that the sons of the Śākyas would simply pick up any garment that fell to the ground;
for this reason, I merely placed it there.
Thinking thus, he immediately gave rise to doubt and regret.
The Buddha then said:
"There is no offense.
You should take it only after careful examination."
There were some boys who took off their clothes, placed them on the ground, and played together. Having finished playing, they forgot to take their clothes and each returned home.
A bhikṣu seeking discarded rags (pāṃsukūla) went there; seeing these clothes, he took them away.
A woman came seeking this robe; seeing that a bhikṣu was taking it away, she said to the bhikṣu, "Venerable sir!
Do not take this robe away."
The bhikṣu replied,
“I obtained it from among refuse rags.
The woman replied:
"This is my son's garment.
He went out to play and forgot to take it with him.
The bhikṣu replied:
"If this is your robe, then take it.
He immediately felt doubt and regret. ...
[and so on] until the Buddha said:
"One should take [the robes] only after careful inspection.
A certain bhikṣu, having hidden his paṃsukūla robes, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms.
Another bhikṣu, seeking paṃsukūla robes, arrived at that place; seeing them, he took them and departed, taking them to the water to wash them.
Having finished his almsround and come out, that bhikṣu went to the place where his robes were kept and saw another bhikṣu washing his own refuse-rag robes; he then said to him:
"Venerable sir!..."
“You have committed a pārājika offense.
He replied immediately,
“For what reason have I committed a pārājika offense?”
That bhikṣu said:
"You stole my refuse-rag robe.
The other bhikṣu said:
"I do not take it up with the notion of grasping. ...
[and so on] until the Buddha said:
"Take it up after having examined it well."
There was a bhikṣu who kept impure discarded rags (pāṃsukūla); the devas rebuked him, and the Vajrapāṇis likewise rebuked him.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
"One must not keep discarded rags defiled by impurities."
"One who stores it commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If you obtain a *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe), you should wash it well to make it clean, sew it well, dye it well, and then accept and maintain it.
A certain bhikṣu took a *pāṃśukūla* from within a cemetery, and was rebuked by a *caṇḍāla*:
"We wished to take these robes, but he has already taken them away. ...
[and so on] until the Buddha said:
"If there are robes within a cemetery that have not been formally relinquished, one must not take them; whoever takes them commits the offense of *sthalāpatti* (thūl'-accaya)."
Not far from the cemetery was a deva shrine, and in that shrine were the robes of those who perform sacrifices. A wind blew them down into the cemetery.
A bhikṣu, seeking *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robe) materials, went there; having seen them, he took them away.
When the people within the shrine came out and saw him, they said to the bhikṣu, "These are our robes; do not take them away.
Our robes were blown here by the wind and fell in this place."
The bhikṣu said:
"If this is your robe, take it and go. ...
up to ... "You should examine it thoroughly before taking it."
A householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to a meal at his home; the community of bhikṣus went there, but the Buddha remained at the place of the invitation.
At that time, the son of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was playing in the Jeta Grove when bandits entered the monastery, seized the boy, and took him away.
Having heard this, a certain bhikṣu thought to himself:
"I shall, by the power of incantations, conjure up the fourfold army to pursue those thieves.
When the thieves saw him, they were struck with fear and left the child behind as they fled.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus said to that bhikṣu,
"You have committed a pārājika offense," whereupon he immediately gave rise to a sense of remorse.
The Buddha then asked,
"How did you save this young child?
The bhikṣu replied:
“I am performing a spell.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense.”
While the community of monks in the kingdom of Kosala was distributing robes, a certain bhikṣu entered a village; this bhikṣu had two resident disciples who both took portions of the robes.
Having taken [the portion] and gone outside, they said to one another,
"Did you take a share for your preceptor?
He replied:
"Take it.
Neither of them knew who was entitled to the portion and who was not,
nor who had committed a *pārājika* offense and who had not.
The Buddha further said:
"There is no offense.
When taking [the items], one should inform the others."
When the Saṃgha of the Kosalans was distributing robes, a certain bhikṣu entered a village; there, a companion took his share of the robe for him.
When the traveling bhikṣu returned, the companion said to him, "I have taken your share of the robe for you."
The bhikṣu who was traveling said,
"I did not tell you to take a share of the robes. Thereupon,
he immediately felt doubt and regret.
The Buddha further said:
"There is no offense of pārājika.
If one does not speak [of the distribution], one should not take a portion; to take it constitutes a duṣkṛta."
While the community of monks in the kingdom of Kosala was distributing robes, there was a monk who was ill. A monk who was nursing him took a portion of the robes on his behalf.
When the sick monk passed away, they did not know what should be done.
The Buddha further said:
"If one dies first and then takes possession [of the object], it shall be returned to its original place.
If one takes possession first and then dies, it is treated like other clothing and belongings."
There was a householder plowing a bhikṣu’s field. The bhikṣu went there and said to the householder:
“Give me my share; if you do not give me my share, do not plow.”
The householder went against the bhikṣu’s wishes and did not stop plowing.
The bhikṣu himself threw himself onto the plow; once the householder had released the plow, he rebuked and reviled him, saying:
"How can you, a śramaṇa son of the Śākyas, do such a thing?"
He immediately gave rise to doubt and regret.
... [As far as] the Buddha said:
"There is no offense."
"A bhikṣu should not thus torment his own body.
Then a certain bhikṣu said to another bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!"
"If one comes and goes together with others to steal property belonging to a caitya, one shall not incur an offense. ...
[and so on] ... until the Buddha said:
"If there is a protector of a caitya, and the value [of the stolen goods] reaches the full amount, it is a pārājika offense."
The resident bhikṣus, for the sake of the Saṃgha, had men plow a field.
Adjacent to this was the field of a householder; the bhikṣus likewise had men plow that field as well.
Seeing the bhikṣu plowing this field, the householder said to the bhikṣu, "Do not plow this field;
this is not the property of the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣu replied:
"Who has witnessed this?
The householder replied,
"A non-human being has witnessed it."
"One should cause the non-human being to speak for themselves.
After this householder had completed his sacrifice to the spirits and made his vow, a mark of proof spontaneously emerged from the earth.
The bhikṣu immediately abandoned his plowing implements; the householder then departed. The bhikṣu took the mark of proof, buried it, and resumed plowing.
The layperson saw the bhikṣu plowing again and said to him,
"Why are you plowing?
You have committed a pārājika offense."
He immediately gave rise to doubt and regret.
... until the Buddha said:
"If the value is full, it is a *pārājika* offense."
There was a bhikṣu who took the fruit-trees of a householder without being given permission.
... [The Buddha] said:
"If it is full [of value], it is a pārājika offense."
The fruit was likewise.
There was a tree growing in a place where bhikṣus practiced walking meditation (caṅkrama), and crows and magpies built a nest upon it.
When the bhikṣus took the wood to use as firewood, the birds cried out, causing a great disturbance in the monastery.
The Buddha then questioned Ānanda, who recounted the preceding events in detail.
The Buddha said:
"One must not take a crow's or magpie's nest; whoever takes one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The same applies to taking, using, boiling, or dyeing for such purposes.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a householder who owned a garden of radishes; a bhikṣu went there and asked for some.
"Give me a radish root.
The householder replied,
"Give me its price."
The bhikṣu said, "There is no price; how can I give it to you?
The householder said:
"If you do not give me my wages, how shall I live?
The bhikṣu said,
"Will you not give even a small amount?"
He replied, "I will not give it.
The bhikṣu then used a spell to wither and kill the radish, and immediately felt remorse.
The Buddha further said:
"One does not commit a pārājika offense, but commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
This is also the case for radish gardens, as well as fragrant gardens, leaf gardens, flower gardens, and fruit gardens.
The horse was eating grass. A bhikṣu held some grass in his hand and walked ahead of the horse; the horse then followed after him.
The bhikṣu moved his body with the intent to steal, but immediately felt remorse.
The Buddha further said:
"He does not commit a *pārājika* offense, but commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
There was a bhikṣu who came with some merchant travelers to the country of Kosala.
Upon reaching a place of great danger and difficulty, the merchants rode their horses while the bhikṣu walked on foot.
The merchants said to the bhikṣu, "In this place of great danger and difficulty, you ought to ride a horse; we must quickly emerge from this peril."
The bhikṣu immediately mounted the horse.
Having mounted it, he conceived the intention to steal, but then immediately felt remorse.
... [The Buddha] spoke thus:
"One does not commit a *pārājika* offense, but commits a *sthūlātyaya*.
There was a bhikṣu who was crossing a river by boat.
There was gold on the boat; he conceived the intention to steal it, but immediately felt remorse.
The Buddha further said:
"He does not commit a pārājika offense, but commits a sthūlātyaya.
There was a merchant who had loaded gold onto his boat to cross a river; the boat then capsized and sank, and the gold chest was carried away by the current.
The bhikṣus were bathing downstream when they saw this casket floating by and took possession of it.
The merchants said, "Do not take this casket; it is our property."
The bhikṣu replied,
“I found it in the water.
The merchant said:
“We were crossing the water by boat, but the boat immediately capsized and the casket was carried away by the current.
The bhikṣu immediately felt regret. ...
[The Buddha] spoke thus:
"No offense.
A bhikṣu living together [with others] took property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions with the intent to steal and transferred it to another monastery; he immediately felt remorse. ...
[The Buddha continued] until he said:
"He did not commit a *pārājika* offense; he committed a *dukkaṭa*.
Some thieves stole oxen and entered a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*), where they tied them up and departed.
When the bhikṣus went to that place, they saw the oxen and immediately released them, whereupon they felt remorse.
The Buddha further said:
"He does not commit a *pārājika* offense, but commits a *duṣkṛta* (or *āpatti*) offense.

In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, various lay devotees made offerings and prayers at a celestial shrine; their wishes were immediately fulfilled, and they offered white cotton cloth (*śukla-karpāsa*) to that shrine.
Kālaṇanda went there because of this and immediately took the robe.
The bhikṣus said,
"You are a thief."
He replied: "How so?
What constitutes stealing?
[The Buddha said: "Taking what has not been given."
He immediately felt remorse.
Thereupon the Buddha said:
"He does not commit a pārājika offense, but commits a sthūlātyaya offense."
The sacrificial rite at Vaiśālī was also as previously described; he departed after tying the golden garland upon the forehead of the deity.
Kāraṇḍava took it, the circumstances of which were as previously described.
There were many women crossing a river; they left their clothes and jewelry on this shore and returned from the other side to retrieve them.
Some even bathed in the water. When the monkey saw this, he climbed down from his tree, took the jewelry, and departed.
When the women returned, they did not see their necklace.
The monkey had thrown it down from the tree onto the ground.
Some bhikṣus were walking up and down not far from there; seeing the necklace, they picked it up, brought it back, and returned it to the women.
The women said,
"Did we give you our ornaments?
The bhikṣus replied:
“We will not accept them.
The story of the monkey is as previously told.
… up until the Buddha said:
"No offense.
There were many bhikṣus dwelling in a certain monastery.
A mouse came out from its hole, took various foods and fruits, and hid them inside the hole.
When the bhikṣus saw this mouse emerge from its hole, they thought to themselves:
"This mouse has taken our food and placed it inside the hole.
The bhikṣus then broke open the hole and took out the various foods, showing them to the other bhikṣus.
"This mouse has stolen our food and placed it inside this hole.
The other bhikṣus said to that bhikṣu,
"You have committed a pārājika offense."
The Buddha then said:
"There is no offense.
However, a bhikṣu should not take food or other items from within a mouse hole."

There was a mouse that took various foods and drinks and placed them beneath the bed of a bhikṣu; in the early morning, after the bhikṣu had finished chewing his tooth-stick, he took this food and ate it.
Other bhikṣus said to this bhikṣu, "You do not go on alms-round; from where did you obtain this food to eat?"
The bhikṣu replied, “A mouse took it; the circumstances are as previously described.
The bhikṣus said:
"You have committed the offense of taking what was not given; you are guilty of a *pārājika*.
... [The Buddha continued] until he said:
"This mouse was the father of this bhikṣu; out of love for his son, he took food to give to him."
"No offense.
A hunter was pursuing a deer, which ran into the monastery.
The hunter said:
"Give me back my deer!
The bhikṣu replied, "It has already entered the monastery; how could I give it back to you?"
He then departed.
The bhikṣus immediately gave rise to doubt and regret.
... [The Buddha] said:
"No offense.
The circumstances regarding the hunter shooting the deer are as previously described.
Furthermore, there was another hunter who shot a deer with a poisoned arrow, and the deer fled into the monastery.
The hunter said, "This deer has already been struck by a poisoned arrow; you must shoot it to kill it, so you all should avoid the arrows.
The bhikṣus did not avoid the arrows, and after they had rebuked them, they departed.
Later, when the deer died, the bhikṣus did not know what they should do. Eventually, the Buddha said:
"It should be returned to the hunter.
When the bhikṣus destroyed the hunters' nets, they committed the offense of sthūlātyaya.
To destroy [the image of] a compassionate mind is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It is the same with destroying a bird-net; it is the same with destroying a prison.
There was a bhikṣu who took the robe of a madman; when that man saw him, he said:
"Do not carry it away.
The bhikṣu replied,
"I shall return it to you later."
He immediately gave rise to doubt and regret.
... [The Buddha] said:
"He does not commit a pārājika offense; he commits a sthūlātyaya offense."
There was a bhikṣu who borrowed many items from a shop. Later, when the owner demanded them back, he resolved not to return them, though he immediately felt regret.
Thereupon the Buddha said:
"He does not commit a pārājika offense; he commits a sthūlātyaya offense."
There was a sick bhikṣu who wished to drink some gruel and also wished to offer it to the Saṃgha.
He said to his disciples, "Prepare some gruel to offer to the Saṃgha and for me to drink.
The sick bhikṣu then gave the price for the gruel to his disciples.
The people said, "We do not need the drink; we shall give it to the sick man alone, and we shall divide the goods.
They then proceeded to act accordingly, but immediately felt regret.
The Buddha further said:
"One does not commit a pārājika offense, but commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
The same applies to *suvīra* juice.
There was a bhikṣu who was ill and possessed many impure items.
He said to his disciples, "After my life has ended, the Saṃgha shall divide my belongings.
He spoke thus to his disciples:
"Give me some cakes," he said.
Terrified by the desolation, she combined the cakes and gave them to him to eat.
Having finished eating, his body became heavy, and he immediately passed away.
After the community of monks had finished the funeral rites, they said to the disciple, "Bring these items here; the community shall divide them.
The disciple searched for them but could not find them. When the monks sought the items but could not obtain them, they each rose and departed.
After the monk Anitya died, a jackal tore open his belly and ate him, and impure substances emerged.
A certain monk went to that place to observe the corpse; seeing those impure substances, he brought them back and offered them to the Saṃgha, whereupon he immediately felt remorse.
The Buddha further said:
"There is no offense.
Furthermore, there was a sick bhikṣu who possessed many fields and houses, and he spoke to his disciples:
"Summon the bhikṣus; I shall give these items as a gift to the Saṃgha, and give separate gifts to those who attend the caityas.
Then the bhikṣu who was attending to the patient thought to himself:
"He intends to give to the Saṃgha;"
"The people of Ceti have made a separate offering;
we may not receive it," they said, and so they did not invite the Saṃgha or the bhikṣus.
The sick bhikṣu then passed away, and immediately felt remorse.
The Buddha then said:
"There is no offense.

A caregiver should not oppose the wishes of the patient; they should act according to the patient's instructions as appropriate, though there may be cases where the patient also follows the caregiver's wishes."
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who fell ill; his disciples summoned other bhikṣus, as previously described.
Also, merchants from Śrāvastī boarded a ship and entered the sea; when a sea dragon seized the ship, some among them invoked the gods, while others invoked tree spirits and so forth.
Among them was a lay follower (upāsaka) who said to the others,
"We should call out Maudgalyāyana’s name.
If Maudgalyāyana thinks of us, we shall cross over in safety."
He immediately called to mind Maudgalyāyana.

Maudgalyāyana then entered meditative concentration and manifested as a king of golden-winged garuḍas standing at the prow of the ship; upon seeing this, the dragon was struck with fear and released him.
The merchants arrived safely in the kingdom of Śrāvastī and, in the presence of the bhikṣus, praised Maudgalyāyana:
"That we have arrived here in safety is entirely due to the power of Maudgalyāyana."
The bhikṣus asked, "By what power?
The merchant then related the previous events in detail.
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana,
"You have committed a pārājika offense.
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"For what offense did you commit a pārājika?
The bhikṣus said,
"You stole a dragon's boat."
He immediately gave rise to doubt and regret.
Eventually, the Buddha asked him:
"With what state of mind did you rescue [him]?"
He replied, "By the power of my supernormal faculties.
[The Buddha asked,] "Is it because of the power of your supernormal faculties that you have not transgressed?"
A caravan of merchants from Śrāvastī was traveling by foot to another country when they reached a perilous place and were surrounded by bandits. Among them, some called upon the gods and others;
however, there was an upāsaka who was a patron of Maudgalyāyana, and he immediately called out the name of Maudgalyāyana.
Maudgalyāyana entered meditative concentration and manifested four types of military forces before them; the bandits were terrified and fled.
The merchants arrived safely in Śrāvastī, the circumstances of which are as previously described.
The detailed exposition regarding the fish is also like this.
After the bowl-carrying Nanda, son of the Śākyas, had finished the *pravāraṇā*, he was wandering among the various monasteries. [The monks asked: "Where did the monks perform their *pravāraṇā*?"
"How much property has the Saṃgha obtained?
When the bhikṣus saw him approaching, they immediately went out to welcome him and greeted him with gentle words.
Once the bhikṣus were seated, he asked them:
“Does the Sangha receive offerings of goods?
He replied, “It does.”
"Bring it here and place it before me.
The bhikṣus immediately went forward, brought it, and placed it before him.
Once it was placed before him and divided, the elder took his portion and stood holding it.
He said to the Elder, "You must not go yet.
Kaṭhina-Nanda was able to preach the Dharma in various ways; he then preached the Dharma to the Elder as was appropriate for him, whereupon the Elder offered him his robe.
The second and third elders did likewise.
Having obtained many robes, they carried them into the Jeta Grove and said to the bhikṣus:
"I have now received a great abundance of robe offerings."
The bhikṣus asked,
"Where was it obtained?
The circumstances were as previously described.
The bhikṣus said,
“This is a cause and condition that has never arisen before.
… [and so on] … until the Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu observes the rains retreat in one place but takes his share of the robes in another, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
The Elder Ānanda had a co-practitioner disciple who was diligent in maintaining his conduct.
There was a donor who had two sons. When the householder fell ill, a disciple of Ānanda went there to inquire after his health.
The disciple took the householder’s keys and gave them to one son; the second son received nothing.
When he was unable to do so, he went and spoke to the Venerable Ānanda; Ānanda then became angry with his disciples.
Ānanda’s disciples then ordered five hundred of their own disciples to perform repentance before their upādhyāya.
The disciples asked,
"How does one perform repentance? He replied:
“Take these boys and girls to the presence of the Upādhyāya; the Upādhyāya shall preach the Dharma to you.
Once he has finished preaching the Dharma, he will leave the children there and depart, and the children will surely weep and cry out.”
The Upādhyāya will surely say:
"Take these young boys away.
You should then answer:
"If you permit me to repent for my disciple so-and-so, I shall take him with me.
He then followed these instructions and preached the Dharma for them; having finished preaching the Dharma, he left the young boys behind and departed.
Ānanda said,
"Take these youths away," and he immediately replied:
"If you will accept the disciple's confession, I shall take him away.
Ānanda then accepted the confession and instructed the disciple to perform a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) confession.
There was a bhikkhu of great majesty who was invited by a wealthy merchant, who said:
"If you have anything you require, come and take it.
That bhikkhu had a disciple who thought to himself:
"A merchant has repeatedly come to invite the Upādhyāya.
I shall go and test him to see whether it is true or false.
He then went there and said:
"The Upādhyāya requires ghee.
He immediately brought out some ghee and gave it to him.
The merchant then spoke these words:
"Those who wish for soup, come and take it.
He replied, "Very well."
The bhikṣu then took the ghee and departed.
He placed a small amount into the soup to give to his upādhyāya to eat, or placed it among the beans; in this manner, he used it for various purposes.
Later, when the merchants arrived at the bhikṣu’s place, they said to him:
“Venerable Sir!
Previously you sent a messenger to take ghee; why do you not send one again now to take it?”
The teacher asked the disciple,
"Did you take ghee from the merchant travelers? He replied:
"Take it.
The Master said,
"You have committed a pārājika offense."
The disciple said, "A merchant invited the Upādhyāya; I went to fetch it for the sake of testing him, intending to give it back to the Upādhyāya as food.
He immediately felt doubt and regret.
The Buddha further said:
"One should take [the bowl] after having informed one's upādhyāya.
(End of section two. The Buddha was staying at the twin śāla trees on the banks of the Vāgvatī River in the country of the Vṛji.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Before the Buddha had established the precepts, committing a transgression first did not constitute an offense.
We have killed many people; we do not know which of these acts constitutes the 'first' [offense]."
The Buddha further said:
"On the banks of the Vālukā River, prior to the establishment of the precepts, there was no offense for anyone.
There was a bhikṣu who, perceiving a human being as a non-human, killed him; he immediately felt doubt and regret.
The Buddha further said:
"If one kills a human being while perceiving them as a non-human, it is a *pārājika*.
If one kills with doubt, it is a *pārājika*."
If one kills a non-human while perceiving them as human, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one kills a non-human while perceiving them as a non-human, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one kills with doubt, it is a sthūlātyaya.
There was a bhikṣu who had been ill for a long time and thought,
"What is the use of this life?
He then went to where a fellow practitioner bhikṣu was staying and said to him:
"Lend me your sword.
He asked, "For what purpose?"
He replied,
"Just give it to me," and so he gave it to him immediately.
He immediately took it and entered the room, closed the door, climbed onto the bed, and sat down; he then cut off his own head, holding the knife in his hand until he died.
When no one had emerged for two or three days, the bhikṣu who had borrowed the knife opened the door and saw that he had cut off his own head and died while holding the knife.
He immediately felt remorse, thinking:
"This bhikṣu has passed away because I gave him the knife.
Had I not given him the knife, he would not have died."
...and so on, until the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
One must not fail to provide a knife to a sick person after having reflected upon it."
A bhikṣu went to the house of a donor, and the master’s wife said to the bhikṣu,
“Come and commit sexual misconduct with me.
The bhikṣu replied:
"Your husband is jealous and malicious," she said. The wife replied,

The Buddha further said:
"There is no offense.
However, if a bhikṣu strikes another with the intent to kill and that person dies, it is a pārājika.
If she does not die, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If there is a monk who employs a means intending to kill a pregnant woman, if the mother dies, it is a *pārājika*; if the child dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If both intend to kill and both die, it is a *pārājika* for both;
if neither dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya* for both.
If a bhikṣu employs the means to cause an abortion, if the fetus dies it is a *pārājika*, and if the mother dies it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if both die or neither dies, it is as previously explained.
If a person has already died, and one kills them again through the power of incantations, it is a sthūlātyaya.
There was a bhikṣu who prepared *suvīra* juice for the community of monks; after many bhikṣus had drunk it and passed away, he immediately felt remorse.
乃至佛言：「不犯。」二比丘共為伴侶，其中一人患病，語其伴曰： Even unto the Buddha’s words: “There is no offense.
Two bhikṣus were traveling together as companions; one of them fell ill and said to his companion:

The full details are as explained in the *Vinaya*.

The bhikṣu then gave him *suvīra* juice; having drunk it, he died, and the bhikṣu immediately felt remorse.

"There is no offense."
There was a bhikṣu who went into the wilderness to contemplate a corpse; he saw a man who had driven a wooden stake from below the path into the ground and said to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable One!..."
"Give me some *suvīra* juice; by drinking it, I shall recover.
The bhikṣu then gave him the *suvīra* juice to drink. Having drunk it, he passed away, and immediately thereafter, [the bhikṣu] felt remorse.
The Buddha further said:
"There is no offense.
A bhikṣuṇī gave five hundred bandits *sūvīra* juice to drink; after the bandits had drunk it, they died. The full details are as explained in the Vinaya.

"One must take care to handle the bricks properly.
There was a community of monks in the wilderness who built a dwelling; they stacked bricks against the walls, as previously described.

The same applies to the construction of stairways and paths.

The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

A bhikṣu was practicing meditation on a mountain slope, while another bhikṣu was atop the mountain; he pushed a rock which fell upon the first bhikṣu, who died instantly. Thereupon, the latter immediately gave rise to doubt and remorse.

"There is no offense.

There was a bhikṣu walking among a herd of oxen when a bull chased him. The bhikṣu fled and fell upon a small child, who died immediately; the bhikṣu then gave rise to doubt and remorse.

"There is no offense.

There was a bhikṣu who suffered from a chronic illness that caused his waist and spine to curve. Disgusted with life, he threw himself into a pit to commit suicide.
Beneath him, a jackal was feeding on a corpse; as the bhikṣu fell upon it, the jackal died instantly, and the bhikṣu’s waist and spine were straightened. He immediately felt remorse.
The Buddha then said:
"There is no offense.
However, a bhikṣu should not act in this manner."
There was a bhikṣu sitting on a bed, and his disciple said to him, "Arise. He replied:

Yet he was forced to rise; as soon as he rose, his life ended, and he immediately felt remorse.
The Buddha further said:

However, if a bhikṣu strikes and kills a madman with the intent of saving that person's life, it is a *pārājika* offense."
If [the patient] does not die, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
There was a bhikṣu who had been ill for a long time; the attendant, becoming weary, said to the sick bhikṣu:

"One does not commit a *pārājika* offense, but commits a *sthūlātyaya* (thullaccaya).
There was a bhikṣu who, having eaten until his food could not be digested, lay down curled up with a swollen belly; the caregiver said:

The Buddha then said:
"He does not commit a pārājika offense, but commits a sthūlātyaya offense."
If one lances an abscess before it has ripened, the person dies immediately, and one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one lances a ripened abscess, there is no offense.
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
If there is a bhikṣu who is ill and requires food appropriate to his illness,
and the attendant does not provide such food, resulting in the patient's death, he commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one provides food appropriate to the illness, there is no offense even if the patient dies.
There was a bhikṣu who tended to a sick person but did not provide medicine appropriate to the illness, as previously described.
Another bhikṣu, being ill, said to his caregiver:

He did exactly as instructed; having gone out, he passed away, and [the monk] committed no offense whatsoever.

... [The Buddha] said:

At one time, a "sword-wind" arose; it was extinguished by pouring water from a meditation bowl, as explained in detail in the Vinaya.

The lay devotee spoke thus:

The assembly of monks said,

The bhikṣus said to this bhikṣu:
"Place the forest-dwelling bhikṣu in a pit.

"He does not commit a *pārājika* offense; he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

An *āraṇyaka* bhikṣu entered and left his house, as previously described.
When the bhikṣus even said,

"One should practice right attention when begging for alms.

A bhikṣu had this thought:

"If one commits a *pārājika* offense but does not die, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If he accepts it in silence, it is a sthūlātyaya.
The householder says to the bhikṣu:

If one accepts [the invitation] in silence, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
A certain bhikṣu, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl, entered the house of a layperson, whereupon the layperson said:

"If he is an Arhat, enter the house.
If he enters in silence, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
Furthermore: "If he is an Arhat, sit and receive water, receive food, receive *khādaniya* (solid food), and so forth; if he is not, depart."
If one accepts [the invitation] by remaining silent, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Suppose a monk, having put on his robes and taken up his bowl, enters the house of a layperson.
The layperson says:

If you are an Arhat, please enter and sit down to receive food," and so forth,
as previously stated.
The bhikṣu replied,

If a householder says to a bhikṣu,
"Your faculties are tranquil, well-guarded,

How does one receive the full precepts?
One who receives the precepts undergoes the *karmavācanā*; because they abide together through the *karmavācanā*, it is called "receiving the full ordination" (*upasampadā*).
There are ten ways of receiving the full ordination:
first, obtaining it without a teacher, which refers to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
2. Attainment through seeing the truths, namely the five bhikṣus;
3. Attainment through question and answer, namely Śudāyin;
4. Attainment through the three refuges.
Fifth, attainment through self-vow, which refers to Mahākāśyapa and the three proclamations.
Sixth, attainment by the five assemblies, such as the Vinaya masters of the borderlands.
Seventh, attainment by the ten assemblies in the central lands.
Eighth, attainment through the eightfold assembly, referring to Mahāprajāpatī and others.
Ninth, attainment through commissioning, referring to Dharmadinnā’s attainment [of the precepts] through the twelve-membered Saṃgha.

If, after the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been established, one receives the full ordination through three utterances or the three refuges, that person does not obtain the full ordination.
If, however, before the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* was established, one received the precepts through three utterances or the three refuges, they properly obtained the full ordination.
Regarding those who come with the words "Welcome": whether they receive the precepts before or after [the formal assembly], they properly obtain the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
For what reason do I grant the full ordination to the *svāgata* bhikṣus?
This is the bhikṣu in his final body; he will never again be a trainee subject to impermanence. For this reason, he has properly attained full ordination.
There are three ways for a bhikṣuṇī to receive full ordination:
first, by receiving the eight weighty rules (gurudharma).
2. Sending a messenger;
3. Receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* in the presence of the two assemblies of monks and nuns.
Regarding those who receive the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), such as Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and others, this matter should be explained in detail.
Regarding the bestowing of the precepts by sending a messenger: this refers to Dharmadinnā or someone similar.

If there are obstacles such that she cannot come out, at that time one performs the *karmavācanā* for her. One who has received the *karmavācanā* takes it and goes to her; having explained it to her, he says:
"Sister!..."
"One has successfully obtained the full ordination.

From that time forward, when the two assemblies of monks are present, one receives the full ordination through the formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations), and thus attains the full ordination.
The eight points of respect and the acceptance by messenger cannot be obtained; this is called "receiving the full ordination" (*upasampadā*).
Question:
"For what reason is it called 'receiving the full ordination'?"
Answer: "One who receives the *karmavācanā* with utmost sincerity and attains realization is said to possess the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
That which is contrary to this is called not possessing the full precepts."
"How should one grant full ordination?
To a human male or a human female who is free from obstructing conditions.
How should one not grant full ordination?"
That is to say: one who has killed his mother, killed his father, killed an arhat, caused a schism in the Saṃgha, or shed the blood of a Buddha;

one who lacks a preceptor; one who lacks robes and bowl; one who has not yet completed the *parivāsa* penance; one who is a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*); one who has defected from another sect; one who is not a male; one who has defiled a bhikṣuṇī; one who lives as a thief in the community (*cora-vāsaka*); one who is less than twenty years of age; one who declares himself not to be a bhikṣu; one who has already been expelled or is subject to expulsion; and all such non-human beings—these are called those with whom the full ordination (*upasampadā*) should not be conferred.
If one confers the full ordination upon such a person, the entire Saṃgha incurs guilt.
That person is called "one who defiles the assembly.
How, then, can the full precepts be obtained?

When receiving the full ordination (upasampadā) from others, one’s name is proclaimed; after the harmonious assembly of the Sangha has inquired according to the Dharma regarding the obstructing offenses, and the formal motion and threefold proclamation (jñapti-caturtha-karman) have been performed according to the Dharma, one receives the full ordination without wavering or turning back—this is called a person who has obtained the full ordination.
The opposite of the above is one who has not attained full ordination (*upasampadā*).
What is meant by one who has not attained full ordination?
One who has not attained it, has not touched it, and has not realized it—this is called one who has not attained full ordination.
Thirteen types of persons can never receive full ordination (*upasampadā*):

those who have committed any of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), those who have defected [from another sect], non-males, those who have violated a bhikṣuṇī, those who dwell as thieves (*cora-vāsika*), those who do not live in common (*asāṃvāsika*), those who were originally unharmonious [with the Saṃgha], those under twenty years of age, those who declare themselves not to be bhikṣus, and those who are conjured beings (*nirmāṇaka-puruṣa*). These can never receive full ordination.
What is *karmavācanā*?
It refers to the motion (*jñapti*), the motion followed by one proclamation (*jñaptidvitīya*), and the motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha*).
For what reason is it called *karmavācanā*?
There are two causes and conditions:
the *karma* of subduing and the *karma* of repentance for offenses.
Furthermore, because it enables one to attain the pure and white dharmas, it is called *karma*.
What are the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) and the *āpattipratideśanā-karman* (act of confession for offenses)?

They are: the act of censure (*tarjanīya*), the act of banishment (*pravāsanīya*), the act of suspension (*niḥsaraṇīya*), the act of confession for offenses (*āpattipratideśanā*), the act of separate residence (*parivāsa*), the act of returning to the original status (*mūlāpakarṣa*), and the act of granting *mānāpya* with return to the original status (*mānāpyamūlāpakarṣa*).
Having performed these actions, it is called the *karmavācanā* of subduing and repentance for offenses.
What is the *karmavācanā* of purity?

It refers to the reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*), the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, the *ābhāṣaṇā*, and other such legal procedures (*dharmakarma*) in accordance with the Dharma; this is called the *karmavācanā* of purity.
What is the matter of the *karmavācanā*?
It is called the "matter of the *karmavācanā*" because it is the causal basis for performing the *karmavācanā*.
What is the locus of the *karmavācanā*?

Because the *jñapti-karman* is accomplished, the proclamation is accomplished, and the Saṃgha performs the *karman* in accordance with the Dharma through concordant action, it is called a *sthāpanīya-karman* (a formal act that cannot be overturned).
What is a *karma* performed in an improper place?

A *jñapti-karman* that is not accomplished, one where the announcement is not accomplished, one that is contrary to the Dharma and lacks the harmony of the Saṃgha, and one that is subject to being overturned—this is called a *karma* performed in an improper place.
What is the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*)?

It refers to a bhikṣu who has committed an offense; he is banished such that other bhikṣus may not perform formal acts (*karman*) or the *poṣadha* ceremony with him, nor may they dwell or eat together with him. This is called the formal act of banishment.
What is the *śamatha-karman* (act of reconciliation)?
It refers to performing repentance according to the Dharma, dwelling together with the Saṃgha, and eating together; this is called the *śamatha-karman*.
What is the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure)?
If bhikṣus engage in quarreling and mutual recrimination, and the Saṃgha has already performed the *kaṭhina-karman* (act of strict admonition) against them, it shall command them, saying:
"If you should do so again in the future, we shall subject you to even more severe punishment."
This is called the *karma* of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*).
What is the procedure for the *karman* of absolution from guilt (*āpattivyutthāpana-karman*)?
If one sees, hears, or suspects that a transgression has been committed, it must be true and not false.

The meaning of acting at the proper time and not at an improper time; being beneficial and not unbeneficial; using gentle speech and not harsh words; and possessing a compassionate mind and not a mind of anger—these are called the matters concerning the *karmavācanā* for the expiation of offenses.
What is meant by "not performing the act of reconciliation" (*an-āpasthāpanīya*)?

It refers to the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), the *nigarhaṇīya-karman* (act of reprimand), the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension), the suspension for not seeing [one's offense], the suspension for not relinquishing evil views, the *parivāsa* (probation), and the *mūla-mānatva* (penance from the beginning). These are called the acts that do not bring about reconciliation.
What is the *śamatha-karman* (act of cessation)?
Confessing and disclosing one’s offenses, humbling oneself, and practicing self-restraint—this is called the *śamatha-karman*.
What is the "matter to be performed" (*kārya*)?
It is because of these causes and conditions that one performs actions.
What is training?
There are three kinds of training:
The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of training:
the training in deportment, the training in discipline (*vinaya*), and the training in the Prātimokṣa.
What constitutes not relinquishing the precepts?

If one speaks of it while insane, in a private place, before a novice, before a non-Buddhist, or before a layperson—and does not speak it before a bhikṣu who abides in his true nature—it is not called relinquishing the precepts.
What constitutes the relinquishing of the precepts?

It is to speak as follows: "The life of renunciation is arduous; it is extremely difficult to be a śramaṇa; I do not delight in being a bhikṣu; I long for my parents and others; send me to where my parents are; send me to the home of a layperson; find tools for me."
He further spoke these words:
"I renounce the Buddha and the others," and so on, until he did not share the Dharma with the elders and others, declaring with a pure mind:
"I do not delight in being a bhikṣu; I have no desire for the duties of a conscientious bhikṣu or the duties of a bhikṣu who seeks liberation."
To speak such words with one's mouth is called "abandoning the precepts.
What is meant by "the weakening of the precepts"?
If a bhikṣu thinks of his household life and does not delight in being a bhikṣu, as previously described, this is called "the weakening of the precepts."
What is meant by "weakening of the precepts" (śīla-kauśīdya) without "abandoning the precepts" (śīla-tyāga)?
It is when one reports the aforementioned matter to the assembly.
For what reason is it called "weakening of the precepts"?
If one takes no pleasure in performing the duties of a bhikṣu, this is called "weakness in morality" (śīla-klāmya), not "renunciation of the precepts" (śīla-tyāga).
What is dispute?
There are four characteristics of dispute:
There are disputes regarding speech, disputes regarding quarrels, disputes regarding offenses, and disputes regarding customary practices.
Why are they called "disputes"?
Because disputes arise on account of them, they are therefore called "disputes."
What is the settling of disputes?
It refers to the detailed exposition of the seven methods for settling disputes, such as the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) and so forth.
For what reason is it called "settling disputes"?
Those four types of disputes are settled, subdued, and pacified by means of the seven principles for settling disputes; this is called the settlement of disputes.
What constitutes a dispute that is not settled?
If five conditions are fulfilled, a dispute cannot be settled.

What are the five? First, not having informed the Sangha; second, that which is not the Buddha’s teaching; third, not having informed the two assemblies; fourth, a bhikṣu who has committed an offense and has not yet received instruction; fifth, the assembly having committed an offense and not yet having repented.
When these five conditions are present, a dispute cannot be settled.
What are the conditions for settling a dispute?
There are five factors that, when fulfilled, allow a dispute to be settled.

What are the five? First, having already informed the Sangha; second, complying with the Buddha’s teachings; third, having informed the two assemblies; fourth, having seen one's own offense according to the Dharma; and fifth, having already repented of the offenses of the bhikṣus.
When these five matters are accomplished, the dispute is extinguished; this is called "the matter of the dispute having been extinguished.
How is it explained?
There are five ways of explaining it, namely:
The Preamble to the Precepts, the four *pārājikas*, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣas*, and the two *aniyata*s, when recited in full detail, are called "recitation.
What is "non-recitation"?
If, when the community is reciting the precepts, the one reciting them is not proficient, then one who is proficient should recite them in the proper sequence.
Furthermore, regarding those who are not capable, one should have others who are capable explain them in succession, continuing until even the most minor portions are explained in order.
Because each explains only a small part, it is called "not explaining" [the whole].
What is "receiving"?
If a bhikṣu dwells alone, when the time for the poṣadha arrives, he should sweep the stūpa, the dwelling quarters, and the hall where the poṣadha is held, and arrange the seats in proper order.
If there is a bhikṣu who comes and has not yet performed the poṣadha, one should perform the poṣadha together with him.
If he does not come, one should look out from a high place; if one sees a bhikṣu coming, one should say:
"Come quickly! Today we shall perform the poṣadha."
If there is no one arriving, when it reaches dusk, he returns to his seat and sits in the proper order, thinking in his mind and speaking with his voice:
"Today the poṣadha is being performed; I too now perform the poṣadha."
"If the Saṃgha attains harmony, perform the *poṣadha* extensively.
This is called "acceptance" (*pratigraha*).
What is the *karma* for a madman?
If a bhikṣu’s mind is deranged and distracted, one should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for him, as explained at length in the account of the Elder Sāgata.
What is a non-deranged *karman*?
Excluding the *karmavācanā* for those who are insane, there are various *karmavācanās* for those who are not insane.
What constitutes the forfeiture of faith-based offerings?
It is when one gives to a person who maintains the precepts and then redirects that gift to a person who does not maintain the precepts.
If one gives to a person of right view and redirects that gift to a person of wrong view, it falls into the category of misappropriating a gift of faith.
Just as with what is eaten, so too with what is taken—even if one takes only a single morsel—it falls into the category of misappropriating a gift of faith.
This is called falling into the distribution of offerings based on faith.
What is non-presence *karmavācanā*?
There are ten types of performing *karmavācanā* in the absence [of the assembly], namely:

The *pātra-nyubja-karman* (act of overturning the bowl), the *pātra-nyubjoddhāra-karman* (act of restoring the overturned bowl), the *kula-kaṣāya-karman* (act regarding a defiled family), the *kula-kaṣāyoddhāra-karman* (act of removing the defilement from a family), the *kuṭi-karman* (act regarding the construction of a hut), the *śrāmaṇera-karman* (act regarding a novice), the *unmatta-karman* (act regarding one who is insane), the *avandana-karman* (act of not paying homage), the *asaṃbhāṣaṇa-karman* (act of not conversing), and the *apratigrāhaṇa-karman* (act of not accepting offerings)—these are called *an-anv-akṣa-karman* (acts performed in the absence of the person concerned).
What is the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act)?
If a *karmavācanā* is performed with fewer than four persons, the *karmavācanā* is not validly accomplished.

A *karmavācanā* for five persons should be performed by five persons; a *karmavācanā* for ten persons should be performed by ten persons; a *karmavācanā* for twenty persons should be performed by twenty persons; and a *karmavācanā* for forty persons should be performed by forty persons.
What are the five dharmas that constitute the confession of offenses and the five that do not?
What are the five [proper] dharmas?

Not in a separate residence, not in a non-common residence, not in the presence of those who have not received full ordination, within the assembly, and confessing fully—these are called the five like-dharmas (the five proper methods).
That which is contrary to the above is called "unlawful" (*adharma*).
What is "white" (*śukla*)?
It refers to a white [motion] that does not constitute a formal ritual act (*karmavācanā*).
When the Saṃgha performs a formal announcement (*jñapti*) for one who is insane, this is called an *jñapti*.
What is a formal act consisting of an announcement (*jñapti-karman*)?

It refers to announcing the matter to the Saṃgha; that is to say, the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, the *ābhāṣaṇa*, the relinquishing of a small bowl, the spreading of grass, and all such matters as these are called a formal act consisting of an announcement.
What is the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*?
It is when, having performed the motion (*jñapti*), one further performs a single formal act (*karman*).
What is the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*?
Having performed the formal announcement (*jñapti*), one performs the threefold *karmavācanā*.
If one performs the *karmavācanā* without performing the announcement, the announcement is not validly established.

In the case of a motion with one subsequent proclamation (*jñaptidvitīya-karman*), if one performs the *karmavācanā* without performing the motion, the motion with one subsequent proclamation is not validly established.

In the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), if the motion (*jñapti*) is not performed but the proclamation (*karman*) is performed, it does not constitute a valid *jñapti-caturtha*.
In the *jñapti-bahula-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and many proclamations), if the motion is not performed, it does not constitute a valid *jñapti-bahula*.
When performing a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, if the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is not made, the action is not accomplished.
Performing more than the required number of motions (*karman*) does not constitute an offense;
performing fewer than required does not accomplish the action.

When the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is being made, if someone among the assembly leaves due to some minor circumstance but does not vacate the area where they can hear the proceedings and remembers the announcement, [the procedure continues].
However, if they vacate the area where they can hear it or do not remember the announcement, they should return and tell the Saṃgha to perform the announcement again.
Before the announcement (*jñapti*) has been completed, if someone rises and departs or leaves the place where they are hearing the proceedings, one must perform the announcement again.
What is the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure)?
If monks engage in quarreling and disputing, and the Saṃgha performs a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* against them, this is called the *tarjanīya-karman*.
What is the formal act of banishment (*nāśanīya-karman*)?
When one has defiled another's family, the formal act of banishment is performed for them through a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
What is the formal act of subjugation (*tarjanīya-karman*)?
If a bhikṣu disparages a donor for the purpose of making him repent, a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) is performed.
What is the *adarśana-pratiniḥsarga-karman* (formal act of banishment for not acknowledging an offense)?
If a bhikṣu has committed an offense and, when questioned, says:
"Without seeing the offense," he is subjected to the formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense (*adarśana-pratiniḥsarga-jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
What is the formal act of relinquishing the suspension (*pratinisarga-karman*)?

When a bhikṣu commits an offense and confesses it according to the Dharma, he is released from suspension through a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
What is meant by "suspension for not abandoning evil views"?
It refers to when a bhikṣu gives rise to an evil, false view and refuses to relinquish it; for him, a formal act of non-relinquishment (*apratinisarga-jñapti-caturtha-karman*) is performed.
What is *parivāsa* (separate dwelling)?
If there is a non-Buddhist who wishes to go forth and receive full ordination within the True Dharma, he should then dwell with his preceptor for four months.
One performs the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for them.

Furthermore, regarding the separate residence (*parivāsa*), once any one of the thirteen matters has been transgressed and concealed, one grants the separate residence according to the duration of the concealment, performing the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
This is called *parivāsa* (separate residence).
What is *mūlāpakarṣa* (reduction to the original date)?

If a bhikṣu commits another *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense while in the midst of *parivāsa*, he is granted *mūlāpakarṣa*, for which a formal ritual of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (one motion and three proclamations) is performed.
What is *mānatva*?
When a bhikṣu has completed his period of separate residence (*parivāsa*), he is granted *mānatva* through a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
Because he maintains a humble attitude toward all bhikṣus without wavering, it is called *mānatva*.
What is *ābhāṣaṇā*?
To raise one from an unwholesome state and place them in a wholesome state is called *ābhāṣaṇā*.
What is the benefit of the separate residence (*parivāsa*) for concealing an offense?
What benefit is there in performing the *mānatva* penance today?
Why is the *ābhāṣaṇa* (rehabilitation) performed?
Answer:
For one who conceals [the offense], the *parivāsa* and *mānatva* are granted; these are the benefits and merits of the *parivāsa*.
The *mūlāpakarṣa* is for the purpose of subduing.
The *ābhāṣaṇā* is the benefit and merit of the *mānatva*.
*Ābhāṣaṇā* (reconciliation), because of purity.
Why is *mānatva* (penance) a benefit of the merit of separate residence (*parivāsa*)?
Because a bhikṣu who undergoes separate residence humbles his mind and becomes subdued; therefore, *mānatva* is a benefit of the merit of separate residence.
Why is it called "subduing by means of the original date"?

It is so that the bhikṣus may know that this elder, having committed an offense with such intense afflictions, now feels shame and remorse and will not do it again; therefore, it is called subduing by means of the original date.
For what reason is the *ābhāṣaṇa* (addressing) the merit and benefit of the *mānatva*?
Having been disciplined and seeking purity, one seeks for oneself the removal of the offense.
The bhikṣus said:
"This bhikṣu seeks purity and seeks deliverance from his offense.
This virtuous and excellent bhikṣu—we shall perform the *ābhāṣaṇā* for him.
Therefore, the *ābhāṣaṇā* is the meritorious benefit of the *mānatva*.
Why is it that *āpavarga* (expiation) is purification?
Because once [the offense] has arisen, one attains purification and is free from fault.
As the Blessed One has said, there are two kinds of bhikṣus who attain purification:
The first refers to not committing an offense; the second refers to confessing an offense according to the Dharma.
Therefore, *āpattipratideśanā* (confession of offenses) is purification.
What is the seeking of an offense (*mṛṣā-vāda-pariyeṣaṇā*)?
If a bhikṣu violates the precepts and, having violated them, confesses them himself but does not speak of them again later, the saṃgha performs the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for seeking his offense;
this is called "seeking the offense" (*paryeṣaṇā-āpatti*).
What is the aggregate of precepts (*śīla-skandha*)?
The aggregate of precepts (*śīlaskandha*) is identical to the collection of precepts (*śīlagaṇa*).
What is the collection of transgressions? Transgressing the *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, and *duṣkṛta* offenses—this is called the collection of transgressions.
What is the category of non-offense? It is not to commit [an offense];
or, if one has committed one, to repent according to the Dharma—both of these constitute the category of non-offense.
What is a light offense?
It refers to that which can be expiated through confession.
What is a grave offense?
This means they cannot be expiated through confession.
What are the remaining offenses?
They are the last four categories: saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, and duṣkṛta.
What is an offense without remainder?
It refers to the first category [of offenses].
What is a terminal offense?
That is to say, the four pārājikas.
What are the gross offenses?
They are the four pārājikas and the saṃghāvaśeṣas.
What is the accumulation of offenses?
It refers to all offenses subsumed under the unwholesome.
What is the emergence from offense?
“You, Elder, have committed such-and-such an offense.
You must confess and repent this offense; do not conceal it.
This is called the expiation of the offense.
How does one remind another of their offense?
"Venerable sir!
You have committed such-and-such."
"One should thus keep such offenses in mind.
What is contention?
If one does not speak with another due to seeing, hearing, or suspecting an offense, this is called contention.
How does one bring an end to strife?
By means of five causes and conditions.
What are these five?
"I speak to you, I address you, I bring forth your offense, I cause you to remember; listen to me.
This is called "stopping the dispute.
What is "seeking the removal of the offense"?
As previously stated, this is called "seeking release from an offense.
What is the "obstruction to the *poṣadha*"?
There are ten types of obstructions to the *poṣadha*, as explained in detail in the *Vinaya*.
What is meant by obstructing the *pravāraṇā*?
There are four types that are contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*) and four that are in accordance with the Dharma (*dharma*).
Those contrary to the Dharma are: one who has committed an offense without basis, an impure person, one of improper conduct, and one who maintains a wrong livelihood.
That which is contrary to the above is called "prohibiting *pravāraṇā* in accordance with the Dharma.
What is meant by "food kept overnight"?

If food is not prepared in a designated pure area (*śuddhasthāna*) within the boundary (*sīmā*), and a bhikṣu within that boundary is unable to eat it, this is called "kept overnight" (*antar-vasita*).
If one has demarcated a pure ground (*pariśuddha-bhūmi*) for food, one may eat there.
What is "cooked within" (*antar-siddha*)?
If a monk does not demarcate a pure ground within the boundary (*sīmā*), and food is cooked within that boundary, the monk may not eat it; this is called "cooked within."
What is meant by "maturing oneself"?
At that time, there was a famine in Vaiśālī, and the lay devotees wished to prepare food for the bhikṣus. They spoke thus:

"If we were to have others prepare it, many people would eat this food, and when our kinsmen and others come seeking to see us, the bhikṣus' progress in their spiritual practice will not be achieved."
He said to the bhikṣus, "Have the *karmadāna* prepare food with this rice and eat it.

The bhikṣus did not inspect it carefully; when visiting bhikṣus arrived, they were supposed to share it among themselves, but the food given to the bhikṣus was so little that their bodies became emaciated.
The Buddha then said:
"I permit the bhikṣus to designate a pure area within the boundary and prepare food there.
Having designated the area, the bhikṣus had the *kappiyakāraka* (pure men) prepare the food.
When the attendants and śrāmaṇeras had finished eating themselves and gave only a small portion to the bhikṣus, the bhikṣus became emaciated from eating so little.
Eventually, the Buddha said:
"In times of such famine, I permit the bhikṣus to prepare their own food."
"Abandoning two instances: storing food indoors and cooking food indoors.
Even during times of scarcity, one must not prepare food for oneself until that period has passed.
What is meant by "taking hold of food"?
Because the bhikṣu lacks a sense of shame and dread of blame, he takes food [inappropriately].
How does he receive food?
If a bhikṣu receives it from a man, a woman, a eunuch, or one with both sexual organs, and so forth.
What is "improper grasping"?
Having already taken food with one's own hand, to receive more from another.
What is meant by "receiving"?
After the bhikṣus had finished eating,
they ate according to the rule for accepting leftover food (*vighasa-bhakṣaṇa-dharma*).
How is it that one does not accept it?
If, after having eaten, one has not yet performed the *pravāraṇā*, it is permitted for the bhikṣus to take the food out.

Just as during times of famine, if one has eaten but has not yet performed the *pravāraṇā*, one may eat provided that the rules regarding leftover food (*vighasa-dharma*) have not been formally accepted.
The rule regarding not receiving leftover food allows for the eating of fruits, such as walnuts and the like.
How is it that this is not abandoned?
It was permitted during the time of famine in Vaiśālī.
What is meant by "eating water"?
The Elder Śāriputra suffered from a blood disorder, and a skilled physician said,
"One who eats lotus roots will recover."
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana took some lotus roots from the Mandārava pond and gave them to the Venerable Śāriputra.
After Śāriputra had eaten a small portion, he gave the remainder to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not eat, saying, "We have already finished the *pravāraṇā*.
The bhikṣus reported this in detail to the Buddha. ...
[and so on] until the Buddha said:
"During times of famine, after having eaten one's fill, even if the *khalupaṭiggaha* (refusal of further food) rule has not been observed, it is permitted to eat lotus roots.
How is this relinquished?
When the famine has passed.
The World-Honored One, traveling from Vaiśālī through various countries, gradually arrived at Śrāvastī.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked Ānanda:
"Regarding the eight matters I permitted for the bhikṣus in Vaiśālī—such as eating things cooked inside [the house], even lotus roots and the like—are the bhikṣus still practicing these matters?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
There are some practitioners who practice it, and some who do not.”
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus.
Having assembled them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“Previously, at Vaiśālī, I permitted eight matters; those were permitted because of the famine at that time, not during a period of abundance.”
"From this day forward, it is not permitted; those who eat [in such a manner] shall incur an offense.
This is called relinquishing.
What is the acceptance of the kaṭhina?
If the *kaṭhina* robe is to be received at this dwelling place, the entire assembly of monks within the boundary must gather, because they share the same precepts and views and are pure.
Furthermore, if monks from other locations hear that the *kaṭhina* robe is being received at a certain place, they may express their sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) and thereby receive it as well.
What is meant by "not receiving the kaṭhina"?
That which is contrary to the above is called "not receiving.
What is meant by "abandoning the kaṭhina"?
There are eight kinds, as explained in detail in the Vinaya.
What is meant by "not relinquishing the kaṭhina robe"?
That which is contrary to the above is called "not relinquishing."
What are heavy objects?

They refer to wooden beds up to *āsandi* chairs and so forth, as well as items made of wood, bamboo, or other materials, such as mats, cushions, stools, bedding, and earthenware vessels; these are called heavy objects.
What are light objects?
They refer to beds made of gold, silver, copper, or iron; and vessels, bowls, clothing, and other items made of gold, silver, copper, or iron. These are called light objects.
What are divisible objects?
This refers to the three robes of a deceased bhikṣu being given to the attendant who cared for him; with the exception of heavy items, all other light items may be divided.

These include iron implements such as bowls, bags, copper vessels, door-hooks, knives, needles, tweezers, nail-clippers, incense burners, incense spoons, incense containers, axes, chisels, and so forth—such items may be divided.
That which is indivisible is heavy property; heavy property is not to be divided.
This refers to items such as wooden beds up to pottery vessels, which may not be partitioned but must be held as the property of the Saṃgha of the Four Quarters.
If the dye belongs to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, those who come shall dye their robes together with it, except for the five great exquisite colors.
As for a golden bed, once the items have been exchanged, they shall be divided equally.
The copper bed is also like this.
Wooden beds and the like are for the common use of the Saṃgha of the four quarters.
Furthermore, there are five things which a bhikṣu must not sell, must not give away to others, and must not divide or break apart.
What are these? They are groves, monasteries, dwellings, bedding and furniture, and the grounds for groves, monasteries, and dwellings.
What are persons and things?
The World-Honored One has permitted the bhikṣus to accept groves for the sake of the Saṃgha, not for the sake of a single person.
What are non-human beings?
They are elephants, horses, camels, *qiú* oxen, and water buffaloes; the World-Honored One has permitted their acceptance for the sake of the stūpa and the Saṃgha.
What is meant by "appropriated objects"?
If they are appropriated by others—
whether in a village or in a forest hermitage, and whether appropriated by men, women, or non-human beings— this is called appropriated objects.
What is "unappropriated property"?
If a village or a forest hermitage is not appropriated by another; if a woman, a man, or a hermaphrodite does not appropriate it—this is unappropriated property.
How does a bhikṣu obtain and enjoy things without receiving them from another?
With the exception of all edible food and with the exception of water and tooth-sticks—this is what is obtained without receiving from another.
What are the robes of a deceased bhikṣu?
The robes of a deceased bhikṣu may be divided and used by the five assemblies.
What constitutes a finished robe?
If one obtains robes at a five-year great assembly, what constitutes a *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robe)?
There are five kinds that a bhikṣu may take: those burnt by fire, those chewed by cattle, those gnawed by rats, water-weeds, and the birth-cloth.
What is nasal irrigation?
The Buddha permitted sick bhikṣus to perform nasal irrigation, as in the case of the Venerable Piṅgiyānī; this matter should be explained in detail.
What is enema administration?
A bhikṣu must not irrigate the lower parts; to do so is a sthūlātyaya offense.
There is no offense if irrigation causes the illness to be cured.
What is meant by "knife"?
A bhikṣu must not treat illness with a knife; if he does so, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
There is no offense if other medicines fail to cure the ailment and it can only be healed by treatment with a knife.
What is meant by "shaving hair"?
To remove the beard and head hair while shaving the hair on other parts of the body constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
What is meant by "shaving the head"?
Monks should shave hair in successive order.
When one of lower rank is shaving the hair and has already applied the blade, the monk of higher rank must not cause him to rise.
Should he cause him to rise, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
What is "eating"?
It refers to the five kinds of seeds.
What is "purity"?
This refers to the five kinds of pure food. What are they?
They are the five kinds of pure food already prepared, as well as the eight kinds of pure, non-turbid beverages.
How does one make robes?
There are ten kinds of robes, and three kinds of dyed colors are used for them.
What is fruit-food?
In Vaiśālī, many fruits were available, and the bhikṣus took them for their own private consumption.
Thereupon the Buddha said:
"You must not take them for private consumption; they should be divided equally."
When the fruit was being divided, one person received it while two or three people shared it, making loud and boisterous noises.
Eventually, the Buddha said:
"It must not be divided."
"If there is a *kappiya-kāraka* who has performed the five-fold purification for the śramaṇas, one may receive food from him.
What is meant by "food of non-humans"?

It is permitted for the bhikṣus to walk, sit, and lie upon floors, steps, and paths made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli in the heavens, and to eat from vessels [made of these materials]; this is called "food of non-humans."
What is the Council of Five Hundred on the Vinaya?
Not long after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, five hundred bhikṣus assembled in Rājagṛha and compiled all the Sūtras, Vinayas, and Abhidharmas.
What is the compilation of the seven hundred [monks]?

One hundred and ten years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, ten unwholesome matters arose among the monks of Vaiśālī—matters that were contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, contrary to the Buddha’s teaching, and deviating from the Buddha’s Dharma; they were in opposition to the principles of the Vinaya and the Abhidharma, yet they regarded these as pure.
What are the ten? They are:

purity regarding salt, purity regarding the two fingers, purity regarding the village, purity regarding curdled milk, purity regarding "thus," purity regarding sympathetic joy, purity regarding fermented liquor, purity regarding habituation, purity regarding the woollen rug, and purity regarding the acceptance of gold and silver.
"What is the purification by salt?
One may receive and keep salt for as long as one lives, and when mixed with food, it may be eaten.
The Buddha said:
"One who eats [in this manner] commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This rule was established by the Buddha while he was in Śrāvastī within the section on medicinal regulations.
Regarding "purity with two fingers": after one has finished eating to one's satisfaction, one may pick out choice morsels using two fingers.
The Buddha said:
"One who eats [at such a time] commits a pāyattika offense.
While the Buddha was in Vaiśālī, he established this rule as an offense within the regulations for eating.

Regarding "purity regarding the village": if one has already accepted an invitation to eat in one village and then partakes in a *pravāraṇā* (self-invitation), one may still go to another village to eat.
The Buddha said:
"To eat [in such a manner] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense."
When the Buddha was in Vaiśālī, he established this offense within the rules for eating.
Regarding "pure curdled milk" (*maṇḍa*): once the meal of self-indulgence (*pravāraṇā*) has concluded, if one obtains curdled milk afterward, one is permitted to drink it.
The Buddha said:
"To drink it is a pāyattika offense.
While the Buddha was at Vaiśālī, he established this rule as an offense within the regulations for eating.

Regarding such purification: if the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for establishing the assembly is performed outside the boundary while those within the boundary merely express their approval, the Buddha said:
"This constitutes a duṣkṛta offense."
This offense was established during the *karmavācanā* proceedings in the kingdom of Campā.
Regarding "rejoicing in purity": one who was not previously informed outside the boundary (*sīmā*) performs the *karmavācanā*, and having performed it, subsequently expresses approval.
The Buddha said:
"It is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This rule was also established at Campā for this transgression.
Regarding "pure through fermentation": when grain has been made into wine but it is not yet matured, one may drink it.
The Buddha said:
"To drink it constitutes a pāyattika offense."
In the kingdom of Caitya, this precept was established because of the bhikṣu Sāgata.
Regarding the cultivation of purity: as for the cultivation of taking life and the non-cultivation of taking life, there is no offense in taking life.
The Buddha said:
"One incurs an offense according to the specific circumstances.
Regarding a *niṣīdana* that is pure of threads: the edge of the *niṣīdana* must not be joined with threads.
The Buddha said:
"To handle a thread is an offense of *pāyattika*.
This rule was established on account of Kālodayin."
Regarding "purity concerning gold and silver": the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī received gold and silver with their own hands.
The Buddha said:
"To receive it constitutes a pāyattika offense."
"This offense was established in Rājagṛha.
When the monks of Vaiśālī practiced these ten matters, seven hundred bhikṣus assembled and abolished this offense.
What is the causal basis for the Vinaya?"

That is to say: the two *prātimokṣas*, the seventeen matters of the *vibhaṅga* and *vinaya*, the thorough recitation of the seven rules and eight rules, the *Ekottara* and miscellaneous *vinayas*, and the common and uncommon precepts.
The Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā, Volume Five;
The Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā, Volume Six.
Translated by Saṃghavarman during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
What is the *mahāśāstrapitaka*? There are four *mahāśāstrapitakas*.
Suppose a bhikṣu comes and says:
