"This is the Sūtra, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma; I have received this Dharma directly from the Buddha’s own mouth."
The bhikṣus should accept these words and not dispute them; they should seek [the truth] within the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma.
If it accords with those, they should praise that person, saying:
"Excellent, Elder! "
"Receive and uphold this well.
If it is not in accordance [with the teachings], you should say to them:
"This is not the word of the Buddha; it is not in the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma."
"You do not understand this well.
This was said in the same manner when two people, three people, or a great assembly came.
For what reason is it called the *Mahāśāstraparivarta*?
Answer:

It is called *Mahāvyākhyāna* (Great Exposition) because it is spoken with great purity and clarity by the Sage; because it is spoken by the Sage; because it accords with the Dharma; because it does not contradict the characteristics of the Dharma; because it grants fearlessness to the disciples; because it suppresses and eliminates what is not the Dharma; and because it upholds the True Dharma.
That which is contrary to the above is called *kāluṣyapadeśa*.
For what reason is it called *kāluṣyapadeśa*?

It is because [the Buddha] wished for his disciples to have a thorough understanding of fearlessness, to uphold the True Dharma, and because in the future age of the final dharma (*paścimakāla*), there will be an increase in wicked bhikṣus who claim, "This is the word of the Buddha; that is not the word of the Buddha. Therefore, it is called *kāluṣyapadeśa*.
What is meant by "corresponding causes" (*sabhāga-hetu*)?
It refers to medicinal substances—such as roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits—which correspond to the cause of the disease; therefore, they are called corresponding causes.
What is meant by "temporal mixture"?

On that very day, one may receive *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for the proper time), *akālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for improper times), *saptāha-bhaiṣajya* (seven-day medicines), and *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya* (lifelong medicines).
Those that are mixed with *kālika-bhaiṣajya* should be consumed during the proper time, because they are subsumed under the category of *kālika-bhaiṣajya*.
What is purity regarding groves?
If a bhikṣu finds gold or silver in a grove, he should think:
"Let the owner come and take it."
What is meant by "purity in the mountains"?
Here, "mountains" refers to trees.
Trees are those whose branches and leaves touch one another, and whose flowers and fruits touch one another.
The area is one *krośa* square; the three robes may be worn according to the occasion until the appearance of the dawn light.
What is meant by "purity of the hall"?
It refers to when the elders sit in order within the monastery grounds.
What is meant by the purification of the land?
If one is in Uttarakuru, one uses the mealtime of Jambudvīpa.
If it is the time of Jambudvīpa, it is midnight in Uttarakuru; for all other directions as well, one uses the mealtime of Jambudvīpa.
What is meant by "purity in border regions"?

In the kingdom of Kukkutavati, people were unaware of receiving food. When bhikṣus possessing supernatural powers went there to beg for alms, those people would take the food and place it on the ground, refusing to hand it over to them.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do,
and so they went so far as to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

“Listen to the five ways of receiving [food] for the bhikṣus: namely, receiving from hand to hand, receiving from vessel to vessel, receiving from robe to robe, receiving from one part of the body to another part of the body, and receiving by placing it on the ground.”
This is called purity regarding border regions.
What is meant by purity regarding regions?
In snowy and cold places, it is permitted for bhikṣus to wear boots and felt-lined shoes; in other countries, this is not permitted.
It is also permitted for the bhikṣus to wear double-layered robes (*saṃghāṭī*) in this region, but it is not permitted elsewhere.
In the land of Aparāntaka, it is permitted for the bhikṣus to use skins for regular bathing, but it is not permitted in other regions.
It is also permitted for five persons, including a *vinayadhara*, to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), but it is not permitted in other places.
What is the purification of robes?

The World-Honored One has permitted ten kinds of robes for the bhikṣus: namely, woolen cloth, *kṣauma* (hemp), *kauśeya* (silk), *kola* (flax), *kārpāsa* (cotton), *kośika* (?), *pattorṇaka* (?), *kautumba* (?), *kauśyaka* (?), and *āvika* (?).
These ten kinds of robes, having been dyed with the three types of discolored dyes, are to be formally accepted and worn.
What is "purification by fermented gruel"?
When the bhikṣus were ill, they consulted physicians, and the physicians said:
"By drinking thin gruel, you may recover. ...
[and so on] ... until the Buddha said:
"One should prepare sour gruel."
As for the method of preparation: take rice gruel and mix it with warm water; set it aside until it ferments into vinegar, then use it as needed.
If the liquid becomes clear and free of turbidity, filter it through a cloth bag so that it is as pure as water.
Having accepted it from the ground, one may drink it until sunset, but not during the first watch of the night.
If accepted during the first watch, it may be drunk during the first watch; likewise, up to the last watch, if accepted during the last watch, it may be drunk during the last watch.
What is the *pravāraṇā*?
On the day of the *pravāraṇā*, if bhikṣus assemble in one place, they perform the *pravāraṇā* within the Saṃgha regarding three matters: namely, what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
For what reason does the Buddha allow the bhikṣus to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony?

It is because he wishes to prevent the bhikṣus from being left alone; to cause each of them to recall their transgressions; to cause them, having recalled their transgressions, to disclose and repent them; to subdue them through words of admonition; so that they may attain purity, freedom from affliction, and peace; so that their own minds may be joyful; and [to realize] "I am pure and without fault."
How does one give the consent for the *pravāraṇā*?
If a bhikṣu is ill and cannot reach the place where the *pravāraṇā* is being held, he should give his consent.
If he is not ill and yet does not go, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If there is fear, or danger to life, or danger to the holy life, or if any of the eight or nine difficulties should arise such that one is unable to go to the place of the *pravāraṇā*, one should grant the consent for the *pravāraṇā*.
How should one who is unable to attend [the ceremony] also grant their consent for the *pravāraṇā*?
How is the consent for the *pravāraṇā* to be taken?
If a person comes to a bhikṣu to grant their consent for the *pravāraṇā*, it should be taken within the boundary (*sīmā*), not outside the boundary; once the consent has been granted, [it is valid].

If there are great terrors or calamities within the boundary, such as threats to life or threats to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and one of these eight causes and conditions arises, then at that time, even if one goes outside the boundary, the *chanda* (consent) is not lost.
What is the declaration of the invitation (pravāraṇā-śrāvaṇa)?
Upon arriving among the assembly, one should announce the declaration of the invitation for that bhikṣu.
If it is so announced, it is well; if it is not so announced, one commits a duṣkṛta offense.
What is the *poṣadha*?
Every half-month, each monk individually examines himself: "In the interval from the previous half-month until this present half-month, have I not violated any precepts?"
If one recalls having committed an offense, one should confess it before a like-minded bhikṣu.
If such a person cannot be found, one should form this thought:
"When I find a like-minded person, I shall confess and purify this offense; thereafter, being pure, I will participate in the poṣadha together with the Saṃgha."
This is called *poṣadha*. Why is it called *poṣadha*?

Because it involves abandoning all evil and unwholesome states, abandoning the afflictions and craving for existence, realizing pure and white dharmas, and completing the holy life (*brahmacarya*), it is called *poṣadha*.
What is the giving of consent (*chanda*) for the *poṣadha*?
It refers to a sick bhikṣu who, at the time of the *poṣadha*, is unable to go among the Saṃgha; he should give his consent.
If one who is not sick gives consent, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
What is the enjoyment of sensual desires?
It is explained at length as before.
The explanation of desire is also as before.
For what reason is it called "consent" (*chanda*)?
"Consent" refers to the act of joyfully participating with approval in the communal affairs of the Sangha in accordance with the Dharma.
How does one give consent?
If a sick bhikṣu is unable to go into the midst of the Saṃgha, he should give his consent (*chanda*).
If one who is not sick gives consent, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If there are ten kinds of difficult circumstances (*āpatti*), he should give his consent.
If it is difficult to arise [from one's seat], one should likewise grant consent (*chanda*).
To grant consent means that by granting consent, consent is established.
When a bhikṣu grants consent, he answers "yes," and thus consent is established.
If one says, "Grant me consent," it constitutes granting consent.
If one says, "I shall grant you consent," it constitutes granting consent.
If one moves the body, it constitutes granting consent.
If there is movement of the mouth, it constitutes consent.
If neither body nor mouth move, one should proceed into the midst of the Saṃgha.
If one is unable to move, the entire Saṃgha should go to that person; they should not perform monastic affairs separately.
If one performs monastic affairs separately, one incurs an offense according to the specific matter.
Receiving the *chanda* (consent) and declaring the *chanda* are as previously explained in the section on *pravāraṇā*.
What constitutes purity?
"Purified" means being free from offense.
How does one grant purification?
It is explained in detail as previously described regarding the granting of consent (*chanda*).
The purity of receiving and the purity of declaring are also as explained in the *Pravāraṇā*.
What is the purity of desire?
It is when, at the time of the Saṃgha’s *poṣadha* and *karmavācanā*, one expresses both one's desire [to participate] and one's purity.
What is the granting of *chanda* and *pārisuddhi*?
At the time of the *poṣadha*, if a bhikṣu is ill and unable to go into the midst of the Saṃgha, he should grant his *chanda* and *pārisuddhi*.
If he is not ill and yet grants his *chanda* and *pārisuddhi*, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a danger to life, a danger to the holy life, or a danger arising from the eight causes and conditions occurs, one should grant the *chanda-viśuddhi* (confession of purity).
Even when such dangers arise, one should likewise grant the *chanda-viśuddhi*.
Regarding "conferring the consent and purification": it means conferring the consent and purification.
When a bhikkhu confers the consent and purification, he replies: "So be it; tell me your consent and purification, and I shall confer the consent and purification upon you."
If one moves the body or moves the mouth, each such act constitutes the granting of consent for the purification (*pārisuddhi*).
If one does not move the body or the mouth, they should be brought into the midst of the Saṃgha.
If they are unable to move, the entire Saṃgha should go to them; one must not perform the *poṣadha-karman* separately.
What is the formal entrustment of consent (*chandapārisuddhi*)?
If a bhikṣu receives the formal entrustment of consent from another bhikṣu, one who receives the formal entrustment of consent should do so within the boundary (*sīmā*), not outside the boundary.

If a threat to life arises, or any one of the eight difficulties up to the difficulty regarding the holy life (brahmacarya) occurs, and one maintains [the precepts] outside the boundary without losing them, this is called purity through desire (*chanda-pariśuddhi*).
How is this "purity through desire" defined?
A bhikṣu who has conveyed his consent and purity (chanda-pārisuddhi) goes before the Saṃgha and declares that consent and purity on behalf of that bhikṣu.
If he so declares it, it is well; if he does not, he commits a duṣkṛta offense, because he fails to show respect for the harmony of the community.
What is a *stūpa*?
The Buddha permitted the making of a *stūpa* from hair and fingernails.
This is explained in detail in the *Vinaya* through the account of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada; this is what is called a *stūpa*.
What are the objects belonging to a stūpa?
They are the fields and houses belonging to the stūpa, and the stūpa erected at those locations.
What is a stūpa-house?
This refers to palaces, halls,
and multi-storied pavilions made of wood, brass, stone, white tin, lead,
or pewter. What, then, is the inexhaustible merit of a stūpa?
The various merchants of Vaiśālī erected a stūpa for the World-Honored One.
Having erected the stūpa, they further offered many articles for its sake.
The bhikṣus did not accept these inexhaustible goods and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha permitted its acceptance and instructed that an upāsaka or a pure person (śuddhakarman) should oversee it.
If they obtain profit from it, they shall use it to repair a stūpa or to construct one.
How does one make offerings to a stūpa?
Clods of earth, white lime, and vermilion.
How does one adorn a stūpa?

One adorns a stūpa with silk fabrics, *ānukaga*, *tugura*, *kujjaya*, *kujipaja*, banners and flags; with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, amber, agate, pearls, *maṇi* gems, red pearls, roses; with aloeswood, sandalwood, powdered incense, ointment incense, lamps, and flowers—adorned with such things and various other exquisite objects.
What constitutes making offerings to a stūpa with music, incense, flowers, powdered incense, unguents, and burning incense?
For the purpose of worshipping the stūpa, a bhikṣu may tie garlands.
What is food? It is when a bhikṣu obtains food while staying in a monastery.
What is gruel?
The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to eat gruel, but they must not slurp while eating it.
What is khādaniya?
The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to eat nine kinds of khādaniya:
Leaf *khādaniya*, flower *khādaniya*, fruit *khādaniya*, sesame *khādaniya*, oil *khādaniya*, flour *khādaniya*, sugar *khādaniya*, root *khādaniya*, and candied sugar *khādaniya*.
When eating these nine kinds of *khādaniya* (hard foods), one must not make a smacking sound with the mouth.
What is meant by "chewing while holding"?
There are five kinds of things that the World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to consume: namely, ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and clarified butter (*sarpirmaṇḍa*).

When taking medicinal decoctions, one should maintain the perception of curing disease, the perception of taking medicine, the perception of excrement and urine, and the perception of marrow and brain.
What is *pūjani*?
There are five kinds; the World-Honored One has permitted the bhikṣus to eat *udāna*, *kulmāṣa*, *śyāmāka*, or fish, meat, and so forth—these are called *pūjani*.
When eating *pūsaṇī* food, one should maintain the perception of it as medicine for curing disease, the perception of it as taking medicine, and the perception of it as excrement and urine.
What is the bowl?
The World-Honored One has permitted the bhikṣus to possess two kinds of bowls.
Iron bowls and clay bowls—
these eight kinds of bowls are not permitted to be kept.
What are the robes?

The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to keep seven kinds of robes, but did not permit them to be given away as pure gifts (*pariśuddha-dāna*). These are: the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, the antaravāsaka, the rain-cloak, the wound-covering cloth, the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), and the life-sustaining robe.
This is called a robe.
What is a *niṣīdana*?
The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to keep one.
The bhikṣus kept *niṣīdana* (sitting mats) for the purpose of protecting the monastic bedding.
Without a *niṣīdana*, one may not sit upon the monastic bedding.
What is meant by "needle"?
The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to possess two kinds of needles:
iron needles and copper needles.
These are called needles.
What is a needle case?
The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to keep needle cases for the purpose of storing needles.
It should not be given to those who lack a sense of shame, nor should it be given to a śrāmaṇera.
What is meant by "relying on a preceptor" (*niśraya*)?
As the Blessed One has taught, an incoming bhikṣu should not first wash his feet and rest; he must first seek a preceptor.
At that time, a certain incoming bhikṣu arrived and heard the Blessed One’s established rule: an incoming bhikṣu may not first wash his feet and rest, but must first seek a preceptor.
This bhikṣu, his physical strength utterly exhausted, sought a preceptor to rely upon; becoming dazed and fainting, he fell to the ground and immediately passed away.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I allow the bhikṣus to set aside their robes and bowls, wipe the dust from their feet, and wash their feet for two or three days, and only after that seek formal reliance.
At that time, the bhikṣus sought reliance as soon as they found someone, and they consequently regressed in wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha said:
"One must not rely on someone haphazardly.
One should carefully examine whether a person can increase wholesome dharmas, and only then rely upon them."
When relying on [a teacher], one should ask other bhikṣus:
"What is this bhikṣu like?
Does he possess the virtue of the precepts?"
Are you able to provide instruction and admonition?
What is the nature of your retinue?
Are there no disputes or litigations?
"Are you able to provide instruction and admonition?
Having asked this, one seeks a formal reliance (*niśraya*).
The procedure for granting such reliance is likewise.
How does one receive formal reliance?
One should bare the right shoulder,
take hold of both feet with both hands, and [proceed].
One should speak thus:
"I, [Name], seek dependence upon the Venerable One.
May the Venerable One grant me dependence."
"I dwell in dependence upon the Venerable One.
A second and a third time he should speak likewise.
He should then reply:
"Excellent! How does one grant formal dependence (*niśraya*)?
One who has not yet completed ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*) shall not grant formal dependence."
Even if one has been ordained for ten years, if they are ignorant and possess no knowledge, they shall not be granted dependence (*niśraya*).
If they have accomplished five qualities, they may be granted dependence.
What are these five?

Knowing what constitutes an offense and what does not, knowing what is light and what is heavy, having extensively recited the Prātimokṣa and already explained it to others, as detailed in the Vinaya—
how does one relinquish reliance?
There are five causes and conditions:
losing one's reliance, returning to reliance, departing and relinquishing the precepts, moving from one assembly to another, and seeing one's original preceptor.
What is meant by "preceptor"?

There were some bhikṣus who had gone forth and received full ordination without a preceptor; their minds were unsubdued, their deportment was not orderly, and when they were ill, there was no one to care for them.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha,
and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit ordination based upon a preceptor (upādhyāya)."
"The preceptor’s instruction and admonition cause the disciple’s mind to attain discipline; thus, they shall look after one another when ill.
Later, when disciples fell ill, the bhikṣus did not look after them.
The Buddha said:
"If one should look at that which ought not to be looked at, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
What is meant by "disciple"?
It refers to those bhikṣus who have gone forth and received full ordination under a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), yet do not come to attend upon or draw near to their preceptor.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

“One should draw near to one’s upādhyāya, serve him, inquire after his well-being, and follow him wherever he goes. When performing tasks, one should inform the upādhyāya; one should perform on his behalf whatever tasks the upādhyāya undertakes, with the exception of four types of matters, namely:”
"Performing the major and minor duties, chewing tooth-sticks, and performing prostrations within the boundary to the *caitya*.
How does one make offerings to the preceptor (*upādhyāya*)?
One should serve, offer, inquire after his well-being, and pay him homage; whatever tasks the preceptor ought to perform, one should carry them out swiftly and not be indolent.
One should have a sense of shame and reverence toward the preceptor; one should honor the preceptor, humble one's mind to seek the wholesome Dharma, and not seek out faults.
If the preceptor has a fault, one should offer counsel; if the preceptor is ill, one should attend to him; and one’s own duties should not be neglected.
What is meant by an *ācārya*?
There were monks who went forth without an *ācārya*; their minds were not disciplined, their deportment was not orderly, and when they were ill, there was no one to care for them.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I allow the bhikṣus to act as ācāryas."
"You should instruct them and tend to their illnesses.
Yet the bhikṣus were unwilling to grant them full ordination.
The Buddha said:
"One should grant him full ordination.
What is a "resident disciple"?
A resident disciple does not attend upon his preceptor. The bhikṣus explained this matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One who dwells nearby should draw near to the ācārya, inquire after his well-being, follow him, and report all actions to the ācārya, except for the performance of the calls of nature."
As previously stated.
What is meant by the preceptor (upādhyāya), the instructor (ācārya), the co-practitioner disciple (sahacara-śiṣya),
and the resident disciple (antevāsika-śiṣya)?
The co-practitioner disciples and resident disciples should regard their preceptors and instructors as their parents;
the preceptors and instructors should regard their disciples as their own children.
What is a śrāmaṇera?
The World-Honored One has permitted the keeping of śrāmaṇeras who are not too young;
the youngest is seven years of age.
If there are those who have committed offenses, they should be made to repent.
If they are naked, provide them with clothing.
How should one deliberate on this?
When first constructing a dwelling or building a monastery, one should first deliberate:
"Will the place for practice be successfully established?
Will it be permanently established?"
Is the place for walking meditation established?
Is it free from obstructions or difficult terrain?
Is there little noise or disturbance?
Having observed in this manner, one should then erect the monastery buildings.
If one undertakes construction without prior deliberation, one incurs an offense.
What, then, are the bedding and furniture?
The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to keep woolen rugs and blankets, whether belonging to the Saṃgha or their own.
How should they manage these affairs?
The World-Honored One was staying at the Ātavi Monastery.
The dwelling collapsed; having seen this, he asked Ānanda, "Why has this dwelling collapsed? Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is because the group of six bhikṣus did not maintain the facilities.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"If you further allow others to manage the affairs, or if you perform only minor repairs—stopping at such things as sweeping the floor—and fail to maintain the property properly, you shall not be permitted to serve as a manager.

Those who are capable of excellent maintenance shall be allowed to serve as managers for the rest of their lives; even if the dwellings are smoke-stained or leaking from the rain, they shall reside there with those who manage them."
The Buddha said:

"One must not serve as the administrator for the rest of one's life, nor may one dwell in a room that is smoke-stained or leaking from rain; a room is called 'new' only by virtue of its twelve-year duration."

If a *karmadāna* constructs a new dwelling or prepares new bedding, the Sangha shall not employ him for twelve years; or eleven years, ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, or one year, during which time they shall neither employ him nor allow him to perform repairs.
What is the sequence?
The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to perform prostrations, inquiries after health, rising to greet, and joining palms in a sequence of superior, middling, and inferior.
What is *sūvīra* juice?
The Buddha permitted sick bhikṣus to drink *suvīra* juice.
This should be explained in detail according to the circumstances of the Venerable Śāriputra’s illness.

Taking medicinal roots, stalks, flowers, fruits, and leaves, place them in a single vessel and soak them in vinegar; once it has become clear and free of turbidity, one may receive it in the morning and drink it until the first watch of the night. For the latter watch of the night, it is as previously stated.
What are "powders"?
The Buddha permitted sick bhikṣus to keep powders of beans, red beans, mūśura beans, and so forth; they must not be mixed with perfumes, nor kept for the sake of their color or fragrance.
However, if one is ill, it is permissible to combine them with other fragrances.
What are medicines?
They are root, stem, leaf, flower, and fruit medicines; medicines for seven days; and lifetime medicines.
The World-Honored One permitted sick bhikṣus to store and consume them, whether for the sake of the community or for themselves.
What are syrups?
They are the eight kinds of syrups that the World-Honored One permitted sick bhikṣus to drink, provided they were strained clean and purified before drinking.
What are skins?
A bhikṣu must not keep skins, nor receive them, nor use them for sitting or lying down, except for leather sandals.
If he goes to the house of a layperson, he may sit but must not lie down.
What are leather sandals?
The World-Honored One has permitted the bhikṣus to possess two kinds of leather sandals: namely, single-layered leather sandals and straw sandals; these must not be made of variegated colors.
What is a foot-rubber?
A bhikṣu must not possess a pumice stone.
What is a staff?
In the Śītavana forest near Rājagṛha, there were many venomous insects, and the bhikṣus were harmed by them.
The Buddha said:
"Once the *jñapti-karman* has been performed, I allow you to keep a staff."
"What is a staff and a pouch?
The Blessed One has permitted a sick bhikṣu to request them from the Saṃgha, and after performing the formal procedure of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, he may keep them.
What is garlic?"
The World-Honored One permitted sick bhikṣus to consume garlic, as did the Venerable Śāriputra.
Those who are not ill must not eat it.
If one eats it while ill, one should act in accordance with the Dharma.
What is a razor?
The Blessed One permitted the bhikṣus to keep razors for the purpose of shaving the hair.
This is called a razor.
What is a razor case?
The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to keep razor cases for the purpose of storing their razors.
What is a door key?
The Blessed One permitted the bhikṣus to keep keys for doors in order to protect their bedding, whether for the community or for themselves, for the sake of the peace and security of the Saṅgha.
What is a door lock?
It is like a door-key.
What is the handle of the fan?
A mani-jewel fan-handle; a bhikṣu must not possess it.
If one obtains [them], they should be taken for the purpose of making offerings at the stūpas of the Buddha and the stūpas of the śrāvakas.
What is a parasol?
The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to possess parasols in order to ward off rain and heat.
What is "riding"?
The World-Honored One permitted elderly and infirm bhikṣus to ride in vehicles; the detailed explanation is as in the Vinaya.
What is "fanning"?
The Blessed One permitted the bhikṣus to possess fans, whether for the community or for themselves.
What is a whisk?
The Blessed One permitted the bhikṣus to possess whisks.
What is a mirror?
The World-Honored One did not permit the bhikṣus to look into a mirror, nor even into water, except when there is an ailment of the face or eyes.
What are singing, dancing, and theatrical performances?
A bhikṣu must not make them himself, nor may he instruct others to make them.
What are these fragrant flowers and garlands?
The Buddha said:
“Monks, one must not wear perfumes, flowers, or garlands.
If one obtains them, they should be taken to offer at a shrine of the Buddha (buddha-caitya) or a shrine of a śrāvaka.
What is the tranquility of the eye in dhyāna?
The Blessed One has permitted sick bhikṣus to keep collyrium for the eyes; it must not be applied for the sake of vanity, but is permitted for the sake of illness.
How is the collyrium applied?
There are two kinds of objects for attachment in the practice of *dhyāna*: namely, copper and iron.
How should one lie down? A bhikṣu who is not ill must not lie down during the day, nor must he lie down under a lamp.
If one becomes utterly exhausted, one should rise and depart, without causing distress to the second person.
How should one sleep?
The World-Honored One has permitted bhikṣus to practice walking meditation and sit during the day to remove the hindrance of drowsiness.
When the first watch of the night has passed, he should fold his *uttarāsaṅga* fourfold, lay it down, and roll up and fold his *saṃghāṭī* to serve as a pillow.
He should lie on his right side with one foot resting upon the other.

He must not let his hands and feet be scattered, nor his mind be distracted, nor his robes be disarrayed; rather, maintaining clear mindfulness and the perception of the light, he should then sleep while reflecting.
In the latter part of the night, he rose quickly and practiced walking meditation and sitting to remove the hindrance of drowsiness.
What is a meditation belt?
The World-Honored One permitted sick bhikṣus to possess a meditation belt for those suffering from pain in the waist or back.
The story of the Venerable Śāriputra should be recounted here in detail.
What is a fastening?
The Buddha permitted the monks to attach fastenings to their robes for the sake of protection against the wind and for the purpose of keeping the robes gathered together.
What is the waist-belt?
The World-Honored One has permitted the bhikṣus to possess three kinds of waist-belts:
namely, the braided belt, the round-woven belt, and the corded belt.
What is the lute?
The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to possess lutes for the purpose of frightening away bandits;
however, one may not strike it except under specific circumstances.
What is meant by "draping the robe over one shoulder"?
A bhikṣu must not drape his robe over one shoulder, except when performing work at an elevated place.
What is meant by "an elevated place"?
There are two kinds of grounds:
the walking-path ground and the vihāra ground.
What is meant by "trees"?
On the road to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain there were no trees.
The Buddha said:
"I permit the bhikṣus to plant trees for the sake of shade and for the sake of flowers; they should be planted in succession."
"What are 'land and goods'?
They refer to fields and land.
It is permitted for the bhikṣus to take possession of fields and land for the sake of gardens and for the sake of vihāras."
What is the forest?
A bhikṣu should take it up in sequence.
What is contention?
They engage in mutual verbal disputes and practice divisive speech; each fights with the other, remaining discordant and unlike water and milk mixed together, each dwelling separately.

They do not act at improper times, they do not act without purpose, they do not act contrary to the Dharma, they do not act out of factionalism, they do not act to afflict themselves or others, and they do not act to afflict both. Such disputes should not be committed.
What is the destruction by dispute? It is when the Sangha becomes twofold;
this is the destruction of the Sangha and the destruction of the Wheel. What is the destruction of the Sangha that is not the destruction of the Wheel?

If one carries out the fourteen matters that cause a schism in the Saṃgha, taking each individual matter of schism—whether it be in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, or contrary to the Dharma and the Vinaya, or even performing the Poṣadha separately within the same boundary—this is called a schism of the Saṃgha, not a schism of the Wheel.
What is meant by the destruction of the wheel but not the destruction of the Saṃgha?
The Noble Eightfold Path is called the wheel.
To abandon the Noble Eightfold Path and advocate other paths is called the destruction of the wheel but not the destruction of the Saṃgha.
The destruction of the wheel and the prior destruction of the Saṃgha are both termed "destruction.
What is reverence?
It is to revere one’s upādhyāya, ācārya, and those of the senior, middle, and junior seats; in all such ways, one practices wholesome reverence.
What is meant by "lowering one's mind"? A bhikṣu who has been expelled should conduct himself as follows: he must not ordain others; he must not confer full ordination upon others;

he must not provide dependence (niśraya) to others; he must not keep śrāmaṇeras; he must not instruct bhikṣuṇīs; if appointed by the Saṃgha to perform duties, he should not accept them; he must not violate other precepts; he must not contravene the *karmavācanā* of the Saṃgha; he must not obstruct the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā* of the Saṃgha; he must not expose the offenses of pure bhikṣus; he must not obstruct the *karman* for ten days; he must not instruct bhikṣus who live in their own nature (*prakṛtistha*); he must not speak ill of bhikṣus who live in their own nature; he must not cause bhikṣus who live in their own nature to recall his offenses; he must not sit together with bhikṣus who live in their own nature. He must always lower his mind and remain respectful, maintaining the awareness that he is under suspension.
The entire saṃgha may not accept any formal acts (karmas) from them.
This has been explained in detail regarding twelve types of persons and seventeen [cases].
What are the various forms of non-residence (asaṃvāsa)?
There are two kinds: [the suspension of] the Dharma and [the suspension of] food.

Regarding the matters to be performed, such as the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against a bhikṣu, the distinction is that he may not receive any formal ritual (*karman*) of the entire Saṃgha, nor may he accept any appointment made by the Saṃgha.
The twelve persons are explained in detail.
If there is one who has committed a transgression against his fellow practitioners of the holy life, the Saṃgha should speak to him thus:
"Do not persist in this."
"The Sangha shall discipline you, bind you, and punish you.
Regarding these two types of offenses, one must confess within this Sangha and may not go outside the boundary.
Only this Sangha can absolve your offense, not those outside the boundary.
If such disciplinary measures do not stop him, his offense is increased further, just as a wild horse is restrained with a bridle.
What is a *tālaṭṭha*?
One who has accomplished twenty-two qualities is called a *tālaṭṭha* bhikkhu.

What are the twenty-two qualities? They are: having diligence as the root; being endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame; being fully possessed of dignified deportment; delighting in upholding the precepts; being well-versed in the Vinaya; possessing great learning through hearing and retention; being proficient in the Āgamas; being skilled in resolving disputes; being skilled in understanding the origins of disputes; being skilled in understanding the characteristics of disputes; being skilled in understanding the methods for extinguishing disputes; being skilled in ensuring that once a dispute has been extinguished it does not arise again; being skilled in the eloquence regarding formal procedures (*kamma*); being free from fear; being capable of properly receiving and practicing through body and speech; when receiving *kamma*, not following favoritism, not following anger, and not following fear; not siding with either of the two extremes; and receiving both the food of the Dharma and the food of material wealth.
These are called the twenty-two *tālaṭṭha* dharmas.
What is the *yathādṛṣṭa-āpatti* (confession according to what was seen)?

If one has previously committed an offense and confessed it, but subsequently conceals it, one shall be given the *yathādṛṣṭa-āpatti*; a formal procedure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) is to be performed.
The procedures to be performed are as previously explained.
What is meant by "training in the precepts" (*śikṣāpada*) for one who has committed a *pārājika* offense?

If, after committing an act of sexual misconduct, one does not conceal it for even a single moment, the bhikṣus shall grant him training in the precepts through a formal procedure of fourfold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). The details are to be explained extensively as in the case of Nandika’s training in the precepts.
One who is training in the precepts (*śikṣamāṇā*) should observe the following rules:

sit below the bhikṣus; offer food to the bhikṣus; receive food directly from a *karmadāna*; stay together with a bhikṣu for no more than two nights; and stay together with one who has not yet received full ordination for no more than two nights.

If there is no one capable of performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) and none can be found, it is permitted for the person training in the precepts to perform two kinds of rituals: namely, the *poṣadha* and the *pravāraṇā* rituals.
One must not perform the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, or the formal monastic procedures (*saṃgha-karman*) with a full assembly.
What constitutes the elders of the Saṃgha?

When an elder enters the boundary, he should instruct the junior bhikṣus, console them, preach the sūtras, transmit the scriptures, and encourage them in meditation, so that wholesome dharmas may increase.
One should always ensure that there is food.
When distributing the food, one should divide it equally so that the assembly may obtain its benefit.
One should employ skillful means to seek it out and should exhort and transform the bhikṣus so that they bring benefit to the assembly.
The monk who is responsible for attending to the sick should seek medicine for the patient;
he should assign someone to look after the patient and should preach the Dharma to the patient, never abandoning them.
The Elder should be fully cognizant of all such matters within the boundary (*sīmā*).
What is meant by "the bed of the Elder"?
"Bed" refers to the monastic compound (*saṃghārāma*).
The Procedure for the Elder:

When eating *khādaniya* (solid food) or *bhojaniya* (soft food), and when the *ghanṭī* (wooden gong) is struck, the elder should go forward and take his seat first; he should observe the deportment of the junior bhikṣus to see who is correct and who is incorrect.
If there is anything improper, one should make a sign so that they may know.
If they do not understand the sign, one should speak to the person sitting nearby to tell them.
If the person sitting nearby does not speak, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should rise and go to speak to them, maintaining a dignified and composed demeanor.
When the food is being distributed, the senior monk (upādhyāya) says:
"Distribute it all equally," and he causes the *saṃghabhedaka* (distribution formula) to be recited.
If a layperson comes, you should have them provided with food.
If there is no food, or if they do not wish to eat, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should preach the Dharma for them, saying: "We have only this much food."
What is the boundary of trees?
It is where branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are interconnected, extending even for one *krośa*.
Within this area, one may wear clothes as desired until the appearance of the morning light.
What is meant by "in front of the hall"?
If there are many bhikṣus in a saṃghārāma, they should divide [the space] in order of seniority.
If one causes distress to oneself, distresses others, or causes distress to both, one should depart.
If the hall is damaged, it should be repaired.
What is meant by a "room"?
If one dwells in a room, one should sprinkle it with water, sweep it clean, and smear the floor with *gomaya*.
One should sweep and wipe the bedding and furniture, and those that are soiled should be washed.
What constitutes bedding?
If a bhikṣu has spread out bedding on an open space and then goes beyond fifty *vyāma* outside the monastery gate, he must not leave.
If one departs, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If there are two bhikṣus, one takes the bed and the other takes the bedding.
What is meant by "the threshold of the door"?
A bhikṣu must not close a door with a sound.
When opening a door, he should first push against it gently; he should enter slowly, ensuring that his footsteps make no noise.
If the door has two leaves, he must not push them together so that they strike each other and make a sound.
What is the inspection of the door?

If one inspects both above and below, one should descend together [with the other] and depart; this is for the sake of ensuring the dwelling is secure, for protecting oneself, and for protecting the bedding and requisites.
What is an empty dwelling?
If there are no bhikṣus in an empty dwelling, one should sprinkle water, sweep the ground, and smear it with cow dung (*gomaya*).
If there are utensils, they should be thoroughly washed and wiped clean.
If there is a *kappiya-kāraka*, one should have them prepare pure grass.
If any laypeople (*avadātavasana*) come, one should preach the Dharma to them.
What is a bowl?
The alms bowl must not be placed upon stones or earthen mounds, nor near the edge of a pit.
When eating, one must not place the remnants of food spat out from the mouth back into the bowl.

One must not wash one's hands or face in the bowl; one must not place it on impure ground; one must not use it to wash with sand or similar substances; one must not leave it wet when storing it, nor let it become excessively dry.
Use it gradually so that it may be used for a long time.
Because it has been damaged, it is difficult to obtain another.
What is meant by "clothing"?
One should regard one's robes as one's own skin.

One must not wear the saṃghāṭī while carrying grass, wood, cow dung, or earth; nor may one sprinkle water on the ground, sweep the ground, remove refuse, or smear the ground with cow dung while wearing it.
One must not sit upon the *saṃghāṭī*, nor cover one's body with it.
The *saṃghāṭī* should be used as a *saṃghāṭī*; the *uttarāsaṅga* should be used as an *uttarāsaṅga*; and the *antarvāsaka* should be used as an *antarvāsaka*.
One must not wear one's robes in impure places.
When wearing robes, one must not carry them on one's shoulders; when carrying the *saṃghāṭī*, it should be cut into strips to form an *uttarāsaṅga*.
The *antarvāsaka* need not necessarily be cut into strips.

If a bhikṣu has no new robes but possesses old ones, and if he has an extra robe—whether it be one of five strips, seven strips, nine strips, eleven strips, thirteen strips, or fifteen strips—he should make an announcement regarding it.
One must not dye it with exquisite colors; if dyed with exquisite colors, it shall be ruined.
It should be dyed with the bark of the *khandapāda* tree or tree bark, and once dyed, it is to be kept and used.
What is a *niṣīdana*?
The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to possess a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), but it must not be made from a small piece of material.
Once the *niṣīdana* has been formally accepted and kept, one must not be separated from it overnight.
What are needles?
There are two kinds of needles that the World-Honored One permitted to be kept: namely, those made of copper and iron.
They should be handled with care so as not to cause damage; otherwise, it will be difficult to obtain replacements.
What is a needle case?
It is for the purpose of protecting the needles.
What is gruel?
The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to drink gruel.
There are five kinds of merit in drinking gruel:
it eliminates hunger, eliminates thirst, eliminates wind-disorders, digests food consumed previously, and brings what is undigested to maturity.
When drinking congee, one must not make a sound.
What is a water flask?
The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to keep a water flask for the sake of purification.
One must not use a vessel for holding food as a water flask.
What is a *kuṇḍikā*?
The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to possess a *kuṇḍikā* so that they might maintain purity.
What is a bottle lid?
The World-Honored One has permitted the bhikṣus to cover the mouth of a bottle with an object.
What is water?
A bhikṣu should cause the water to be purified; he should carefully strain the water, inspect it well, and ensure there are no insects.
Having washed his hands clean and put on clean robes, he should strain the water; he must not strain the water with unclean hands or while wearing unclean robes.
What is a drinking vessel?
The World-honored One has permitted the bhikṣus to possess drinking vessels, provided they keep them clean.
What is food?
There are five kinds of *pūjani* (soft foods). When eating any one of these *pūjanis*, one should contemplate the food: "From where does this food come?
It comes from the granary."
What is the cause of the granary?
The granary emerges from the earth.
What, then, is the cause of the earth?
Since the seed was produced through the combination of excrement and urine, one now returns once more to nourish this body of excrement.
When picking up a morsel, one should conceive it as excrement; with right mindfulness present before them, they should eat without a distracted mind.

One should eat with the thought that it is a meal received as an offering, with the thought that it is obtained from another, with the thought of being ill, and with the thought that it is obtained through specific causes and conditions; only then should one eat.
One should further observe whether one is eating apart from the community, and one should also observe whether the *pravāraṇā* has been performed or not.
What is the time for eating?

When eating the five kinds of formal meals, at the time the *ghanṭā* is struck, one should adjust one’s robes and maintain a dignified and solemn demeanor; upon entering the assembly, one must not make any speaking sounds.
What is meant by "food"?
One should not take more than one's share to give to others, except for one’s parents and brothers.
When guests arrive at the monastery, or when there are the sick or women who are pregnant, one should, having established right mindfulness, provide them with food.
One should give a single morsel to an animal.
To one who wishes to leave the household life and who will be of benefit to the community, one should give [more].
How should one receive food?
One should receive food with a single-minded focus, without a distracted mind.
One should receive food with right mindfulness, exactly as it is eaten and exactly as it is taken.
How does one beg for food?
The detailed explanation is as given in the Vinaya.
What is meant by "requesting food"?
When a bhikṣu requests food, he must not cover it with various fine things, nor should he defile it with impurities.
One should know the proper timing.
What is a forest-dwelling bhikṣu?
A forest-dwelling bhikṣu should always speak with pleasant words, maintain a smile, and stand before others without knitting his brows.
He keeps a pure water vessel filled with water;
he keeps a fire-gem and a moon-gem.
What is a forest-dwelling elder?

The forest-dwelling elder shall instruct and admonish the junior bhikṣus and preach the Dharma; he shall instruct them by means of the forest-dweller’s way of life, so that the forest-dweller’s way of life may increase.
What is a village?
Regarding monks in a village, it is as previously described.
When laypeople come, one should preach the Dharma for them according to one's ability.
What is the senior monk of a village?
The senior monk of a village is as previously described.
What is a visiting bhikṣu?
If a visiting bhikṣu arrives, he should stand silently in the designated place, maintaining his deportment with composure as previously described.
What is a visiting senior (upādhyāya)?
A visiting senior should observe his fellow bhikṣus and send a messenger to inform the resident bhikṣus, requesting a room and bedding.
What is the procedure for traveling?
When intending to travel the next day, one should inform the Upādhyāya and Ācārya, saying:
"I am going toward such-and-such a direction, to such-and-such a country."
"If permission to depart is granted, one may go; if it is not granted, one must not go.
One should sprinkle and sweep the room where one stayed and dust the bedding before departing."
What is the practice of the senior elder?
A senior elder bhikṣu should observe the junior bhikṣus, ensuring that the junior bhikṣus go first and the elder goes behind, remaining mindful throughout and forgetting nothing.
Instructing the young bhikṣus: do not allow them to be restless or playful.

They should seek out trading companions; they should examine the regions and countries; they should examine their dwelling places; they should examine their bedding and furniture; and they should examine whether their fellow bhikṣu-companions are compatible or incompatible.
Do not abandon one another midway due to illness or pain, nor depart without having made an investigation, for by doing so you will incur an offense according to the circumstances.
How should one wash the feet?
If a bhikṣu has finished washing his feet, he should pour water into the vessel when it becomes empty.
What is the procedure for washing the feet of a senior elder (sthavira)?
If a junior bhikṣu has already washed [the elder's feet] first, he should provide water; the elder must not be made to rise, as his feet have already been rinsed.
How is the assembly conducted?
On the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day, if one is not ill, one should assemble in one place to preach the Dharma.
How is the Elder (upādhyāya) assembled?
If the *gandī* is struck, the senior monk (*sthavira*) shall go forward and sit at the head.
After remaining silent for a short while, he should preach the Dharma himself.
If he is unable to do so, he should have another bhikṣu preach it.
If laypeople come, one should preach the Dharma for them.
If followers of external paths come, one should preach the Dharma to attract them, speaking with a sincere heart and without pride or arrogance.
How does one preach the Dharma?

If a bhikṣu is to preach the Dharma, he should respect the assembly and love the assembly; with a humble mind and utmost sincerity, he should preach for them, fully endowed with both meaning and phrasing, without his mind being distracted.
Out of compassion and sympathetic concern, he joyfully expounded it for them, not for the sake of food or drink.
He taught them in due order, honoring the Dharma and preaching the Dharma for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of wealth or profit.
What is meant by a "senior elder who expounds the Dharma"?
One should examine whether the person expounding the Dharma is teaching the Dharma or what is not the Dharma.
If they teach what is not the Dharma, one should admonish them; if they are mistaken, one should set them right.
If one is to preach the Dharma, one should praise and extol it.
What constitutes "inappropriate time"?
When one wishes to go out, one should inform the upādhyāya and the ācārya.
"I wish to travel to such-and-such a place or village.
Having said this, he departs.
What is an untimely assembly of the Saṃgha?
Except on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days, at all other times of assembly, whatever business the Saṃgha has to attend to,
if there is a distribution of goods, one should assemble quickly and take their seats as soon as the *ghanṭā* is struck.
What is the improper conduct of the Elder when the assembly gathers at an untimely hour?
When the *ghanṭā* is struck, the Elder walks in front and sits in front.
He should act in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.
What is *bhāṣya*?

In the city of Rājagṛha, various non-Buddhist practitioners gather in one place on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month to chant their recitations; thus they obtain much material support and their followers increase.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, who had faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
The various non-Buddhist practitioners gather in one place on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days to chant and recite; they receive much gain and support, and their followers increase.”

May the World-Honored One permit the bhikṣus to assemble in one place on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month to preach the Dharma and chant hymns; thus shall they obtain offerings and their followers increase, the donors shall gain merit, and the bhikṣus shall attain swift eloquence—for the sake of upholding the Buddha-dharma and ensuring that the True Dharma abides for a long time.
The Buddha said,
"I permit the bhikṣus to assemble in one place on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days to chant and preach the Dharma.
However, the bhikṣus chanted with ordinary voices, which did not satisfy the assembly.
The assembly said:
"It would be well if the Buddha permitted the bhikṣus who possess beautiful voices to chant and recite.
... until the Buddha spoke:
"Listen to the bhikṣus chanting with beautiful voices.
The bhikṣus then chanted with low voices, and the assembly could not hear them.
The assembly said:
"It would be well if the Buddha permitted standing *bhāṣaṇa* (chanting).
... Eventually, the Buddha said:
"I permit the bhikṣus to perform standing *bhāṣaṇa*."
When the bhikṣus had finished reciting the sūtras in full length, the assembly said, "It would be well if the Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to recite only the essential points in brief. ...
until the Buddha spoke:
"Listen as I briefly recite the essential meaning for you, O bhikṣus.
When the bhikṣus had finished this brief recitation, doubt and regret arose in their minds:
"Have we not failed to preserve the Sūtras?"
The Buddha then said:
"From among these, you should explain what constitutes the essential meaning; as for the rest of the sūtras, you should uphold them without forgetting.
When the bhikṣus chanted only half [of the verses], the Buddha said:
"One must not chant in fragments.
To chant in fragments is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Several bhikṣus were chanting together in pairs, causing disturbance to the assembly.
The Buddha said:
"Two people may not chant together.
To chant together constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The bhikṣus each took their own groups away with them. The Buddha said:
"You must not take groups away with you.
If you do so, you commit an offense according to the specific circumstances."
There is no offense if one departs of one's own accord, or if one departs for reasons other than for the sake of the Dharma.
Furthermore, when the bhikṣus supported themselves by means of preaching the Dharma,
the Buddha said:
"One must not seek one's livelihood by preaching the Dharma.
If there is no one among the assembly capable of chanting, they should be appointed in turn.
If there is absolutely no one, each person should recite a single verse."
What is "not chanting"?
If there is one capable [of chanting] among those present, they should be requested to speak; if they are requested but do not speak, they commit a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
What is "seeking the rainy season retreat"?
When intending to enter the rains retreat (*varṣā*), one should carefully deliberate before doing so: "Is consent obtained for this dwelling place?
Will it be a pleasant stay?
Can we speak and sit together [with the other residents]?"
Furthermore, is there food and drink suitable for the illness that is easy to obtain?
Can medicine be obtained when one is ill?
And is there someone to attend to the patient?
"Are there those who uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, the Mātṛkā, and the Abhidharma?
Are there no monks engaged in quarreling or mutual dispute?
Is the Saṃgha not divided?"
Having deliberated in this manner, one enters the rains retreat (*varṣā*).
How does one enter the retreat? During the retreat, unless there is a specific necessity, one must not go beyond the boundary even for a single night.
If there is a matter for which one must leave, one should receive the seven-day authorization (*saptāha-vidhi*).
Whether it be for the sake of a stūpa, or for the illness of one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or teacher (*ācārya*), or for the sake of the Dharma—for such causes and conditions, departure is permitted.
What is the procedure for the senior monk (*sthavira*) during the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*)?

The senior monk of the retreat should take note of the monasteries (*vihāra*) and meditation caves; those that are dilapidated, he should have them repaired and encourage others to manage and maintain them.
What is meant by "the conclusion of the rainy season retreat"?
There are three matters regarding the conclusion of the rainy season retreat, namely:
robes, bowls, and the *kaṭhina* robe.
If one obtains [the cloth] during the *varṣā* retreat, it may or may not be used as a *kaṭhina* robe.
What constitutes the "assembly"?
A bhikṣu should observe the assembly: who possesses good deportment?
Who has improper conduct?
Whoever has improper conduct should be subdued—
be they from the kṣatriya assembly or even the householder assembly.
How does one enter an assembly?
One enters the assembly of kṣatriyas in this way, the assembly of brahmins in this way, the assembly of śramaṇas in this way, and the assembly of householders in this way.
Thus one should walk, thus stand, thus sit, thus speak, and thus remain silent.
What is meant by "during the rains retreat"?

During the rains retreat, a bhikṣu must not engage in various kinds of worldly discourse, namely: talk of state affairs and ministers, battles and victory or defeat, animals and hungry ghosts, or matters such as male and female desire, food, and drink.
What is the procedure for the senior monk during the rains retreat?
The senior monk during the rains retreat should observe whether the assembly is at ease or not.
If they are at ease, he should remain silent; if they are not at ease, he should preach the Dharma accordingly.
What is the *poṣadha*?
There are five kinds of *poṣadha*:

the recitation, the non-recitation, the granting of purity (*pārisuddhi*), the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), and the formal matter of the *poṣadha*. These are explained in detail as in the *Poṣadha-vastu*.
How is the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha) performed?
There are five ways of reciting the precepts, as explained extensively above.
What is meant by "reciting the precepts"?
The bhikṣu reciting the precepts should do so skillfully and in proper sequence, ensuring that no words or phrases are omitted.
He should examine himself: "Have I committed any transgressions against the precepts since the fifteenth day of the previous month?"
One who has committed an offense should confess it as soon as they obtain consent; if consent cannot be obtained, they should reflect:
"I shall confess it when I obtain consent, practicing in accordance with the *pātimokkha*."
What is the Elder who recites the Prātimokṣa?
When the ghaṇṭā is struck, he should examine himself: "Have I not transgressed the precepts?
If he has transgressed the precepts, it is as previously explained.
What is meant by "senior elder"?

A senior elder bhikṣu should look after junior bhikṣus; when junior bhikṣus are in the places for defecation and urination, he should watch over them so that they do not commit any act that violates the precepts.
When the *gandī* is struck, [the monks] assemble; among them, what is meant by "senior seats" (*upasthāyaka*)?
As for "middle seats" (*madhyama*), the bhikṣus in the middle seats follow the senior seats into the village.
If the senior monk has not yet finished his bodily functions, one should wait if he has gone a short distance;
if he has not come out but has gone far away, one should wait for him to return.
What is meant by a junior monk?

When it is time for the meal, the junior bhikṣu should bring out the food; when water is being served, he should observe whether it is early or late and wait for the senior bhikṣu; he should sweep the ground and smear it with cow dung, spread out the bedding, and provide water and food.
When it is time to eat from the alms bowl, one should again serve water and invite [the guest] to eat.
One should kindle fire and fetch water within the bathhouse; one should take firewood and place it in the bathhouse, and procure oil, cow dung, and powdered earth.
When the water accepts the body’s scrubbing, it is called "scrubbing the body," and one should discard the excrement.
All heavy tasks should be performed.
What is a bathhouse?
Lowering his voice, he entered the bathhouse and adjusted his deportment.
He thought, "How does one bathe?
The World-Honored One has permitted bhikṣus to bathe.
There are five kinds of merit in bathing, as stated in the sūtras.
Furthermore, there are another five kinds of merit, namely: the removal of wind, the removal of cold, the removal of heat, the removal of impurities, and the arousal of disenchantment.
When bathing, one should inform the Upādhyāya and Ācārya.
When bathing, one should sit behind the senior monks (sthavira) and not in front of them.
One should adjust the water toward the fire so that it is temperate; if it is too cold or too hot, one should inform others.
Without having informed one's preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya), one must not rub another’s body, nor may one allow one’s own body to be rubbed.
If there is a place where the preceptor or teacher feels aversion, one must not frequent it.
In the bathhouse, items such as seats and vessels should be lifted and returned to their original places, as explained in detail in the Vinaya.
What is the procedure for the senior monk (upādhyāya) of the bathhouse?
When the junior monks have already finished bathing and are perspiring, the senior monk must not cause them to rise.
What is an upādhyāya?

An upādhyāya should instruct and admonish his disciple, teach him the recitation of the sūtras and their doctrinal meanings, guide and direct him to practice seated meditation, instruct him to distance himself from evil associates and draw near to virtuous friends, and further provide him with robes, alms bowls, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
One should take charge of those who have transgressed the precepts and instruct them to repent their errors.
What is meant by a "disciple"?

A disciple should feel shame before the upādhyāya, should serve and attend to him, and should inform him of all that he does. He should stand in a respectful posture before the upādhyāya and follow him when walking. He should seek robes, bowls, and other necessities for the upādhyāya, as previously explained for the case of a disciple.
If wholesome qualities do not increase, one should say to the preceptor:
"Give me [the charge of] such-and-such a bhikṣu.
The preceptor should then observe this bhikṣu: "How does this bhikṣu conduct himself?"
"What are his attendants like?
Is he capable of providing instruction and admonition?
Having deliberated thus, he sent him away.
If he does not further increase [in virtue], he should depart.
What, O Ācārya? The detailed explanation is as before.
What is a resident disciple?
It is explained in detail as being like a co-resident disciple.
What is a śrāmaṇera?
It is also like a co-resident disciple.
The distinction is that the śrāmaṇera should purify flowers, fruits, tooth-sticks, and grass, and cause them to be rendered pure.
How does one administer punishment?
If a bhikṣu has committed an offense, one should employ skillful means to question him so that he confesses it himself.

If he does not confess it himself, one must not immediately issue the formal act for the removal of the offense; first, one should seek companions—such as a king, a prince, or a royal minister who possesses great power.
Once a companion has been found, one may then depart from that offense.
What is a junior monk (*paścācchramaṇa*)?
A junior monk must not walk ahead, must not sit ahead, must not speak unless he has informed the senior monk (*sthavira*), and when questioned, he should respond to the senior monk.
While speaking, one must not interrupt with irrelevant talk.

When a senior elder speaks what is contrary to the Dharma, one should offer admonition; when one speaks the Dharma, one should express approval; and when receiving offerings in accordance with the Dharma, one should accept them.
How does one enter a house?
When a bhikṣu enters the home of a layperson, he must not engage in playful jesting, nor must he cast his eyes about.
How does one enter the dwelling of a layperson?
When a bhikṣu enters the home of a layperson with a lack of mindfulness, there are five kinds of faults:

entering and sitting without prior announcement; sitting while eating in a household; sitting in a secluded or concealed place; eating separately from the community; and preaching the Dharma to women without a pure attendant present.
One who possesses right mindfulness is free from such faults.
How should one enter a house and sit?

A bhikṣu entering a house and sitting there must not speak of animals, their lands, food, drink, and so forth; rather, he should preach the Dharma for them, causing them to enter into right view, practice giving, subdue the sense faculties, cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), observe the Uposatha, receive the precepts, and take the three refuges.
What is the elder of a layperson’s household?
An elder of a layperson’s household should instruct and admonish young bhikṣus so that they do not engage in frivolous play.
How should one converse? When a visiting bhikṣu arrives, a resident bhikṣu should first extend a greeting with a friendly disposition.
"Welcome, welcome," he said with gentle and affectionate words,
smiling as he appeared before him, without frowning.
When a visiting bhikṣu arrives, one should greet him with joy and ask:
"Are you not weary from the road?
Have you not missed the proper time for food and drink?"
"Are you not greatly fatigued?
One should ask how many years of seniority (*kṣānti*) he has.

If he is a *sthavira*, one should rise and pay homage, take his robe and bowl, prepare a seat, provide water for washing his feet, offer whatever sustenance one is able according to one's means, and provide him with excellent bedding.
How should one inquire after others?
If a visiting bhikṣu arrives at a monastery, he should not immediately seek a room or bedding; rather, he should sit quietly in one place and maintain his deportment with composure.
What is meant by "in the air"?
In the air, no ritual action (karmavācanā) whatsoever may be performed.
A bhikṣu must not walk in the air, except when the morning star has risen.
During the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), except for the acceptance of the seven-night [extension],
what is the *kaṭhina*? If a bhikṣu accepts the *kaṭhina*, there are seven benefits:

Keeping robes according to one's own preference; entering a village without wearing the saṃghāṭī; eating apart from the community; eating repeatedly; entering a village without announcing one’s arrival; the benefits of the kaṭhina robe; and entering a village wearing a plain robe.
What is walking meditation (*caṅkrama*)?

When a bhikṣu is practicing walking meditation, if there is a senior elder (*sthavira*) ahead of him, he should announce his presence; he must not sway his body as he walks, nor walk too fast, nor bow his head too low or hunch his shoulders.
One should restrain the sense faculties so that the mind does not wander toward external objects.
One should walk with upright posture; for those who cannot maintain an upright gait, one should use a cord as a guide.
What is a water-strainer?
One must not travel a long distance without a water-strainer.
This does not apply if the river water is naturally pure, if the spring water is naturally pure, or within a distance of half a *yojana*.
If monasteries are situated in close succession within that half-*yojana* range, one commits no offense even if one does not carry a water-strainer.
What is the lower wind?
When the lower wind issues forth, it must not make a sound.
What is entering the latrine?
When a bhikṣu enters the latrine, he should first snap his fingers as a signal to alert those inside.
He should enter with right mindfulness, properly adjusting his robes and maintaining correct posture, keeping his body centered within the space.
Those who wish to leave may do so; those who are unwilling to leave should not be forced out.
What is meant by "near the latrine"?

A bhikṣu must not wash clothes, cut cloth, sew, or dye clothes near the latrine; he must not hold a sūtra, recite a sūtra, make a formal announcement (*jñapti*), or perform walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). He must not perform any such activities, except for those directly connected to the latrine.
What is meant by "using the latrine slippers"?
A bhikṣu should step onto them slowly and must not soil the slippers.
What is meant by "sitting on the latrine seat"?
If a junior bhikṣu enters first, he must not be asked to leave.
How is one to wash?

If a bhikṣu does not wash after defecating or urinating, he is not permitted to perform prostrations or receive them, nor may he sit or lie upon the bedding and seats of the Saṃgha, except in places where water is unavailable.
If one acts thus, one will be reviled by non-human beings and the water deities.
Or, one may take medicine.
What is the place for washing hands after having performed the great excretion?
One must not wash clothes or similar items near the hand-washing area, as previously stated.
When washing one's sandals at the washing station, one should do so slowly and carefully, ensuring that the sandals are not stained or made wet.
What is the rule for urination?
A bhikṣu must not urinate here and there; he should dig a pit in one specific place.
What is the place for urination?
One must not wash clothes or perform similar acts near the place for urination, as previously stated.
What is meant by "urinating on a sandal"?
A bhikṣu should urinate slowly and carefully so as not to soil or dampen his sandals.
What is the "senior monk's urination"?
Once a junior monk has finished urinating, one must not make him rise.
What is the "straw tally" (śalākā)?
One must not scrape with a sharp instrument, nor wipe with grass.
One should use a fine, soft, and smooth object, such as stone or wood.
How should one spit?
One must not make a sound while spitting; one must not spit in front of a senior monk, nor on clean ground, nor before a meal.
If it cannot be endured, one should rise and move away so as not to cause distress to others.
What are the vessels?
The Blessed One permitted the bhikṣus to possess two kinds of vessels:
a vessel for fumigating the bowl and a spittle vessel.
One should guard it well so as not to let it be damaged or ruined;
once it is obstructed or discarded, it is difficult to find another.
What is a tooth-stick?
The tooth-stick must not be too large or too small, nor too long or too short.
The superior length is twelve finger-widths; the inferior is six finger-widths.
One must not chew the tooth-stick in front of a senior monk.
There are three matters that should be attended to in a secluded place:
namely, defecating, urinating, and chewing a tooth-stick.
One must not chew a tooth-stick in a clean place, under a tree, or beside a wall.
What is the method for cleaning the teeth?
One should not use a tool that is too sharp, nor should one pierce between the teeth too hastily; rather, one should pick gently so as not to injure the gums.
What is the method for scraping the tongue?
One must not use sharp objects to scrape [the teeth], nor should one scrape too hastily; one should do so slowly and gently so as not to injure the tongue.
How should one clean the ears?
One must not use sharp objects to pick them, nor should one pick them too hastily; one must not cause injury to the flesh.
What is decorum?
All the merits produced by a śramaṇa constitute decorum.
That which is contrary to the above is called lack of decorum.
What are the three aggregates?
They are the aggregate of receiving the precepts, the aggregate of correspondence, and the aggregate of deportment.
The Buddha’s exposition of the *Mātṛkā* has been well-recited.
The Sarvāstivāda Vinaya-mātṛkā, Volume Six;
The Sarvāstivāda Vinaya-mātṛkā, Volume Seven.
Translated by Saṃghavarman during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
"As the Buddha has taught that five *vinaya-dhara* masters from a border region may confer full ordination,
if there are ten such *vinaya-dhara* masters and five receive the precepts, will they obtain the precepts?"
The Buddha said:
"If one has received full ordination, the bhikṣus may reprove him for his offense.
"As the Buddha has taught, if a robe exceeds ten nights [without being processed], it is an *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
How does one obtain an extra robe?
It means that if it has entered one's hand, or if it is upon one's knee or shoulder, one forms the thought: "This is my robe."
“Monks, may one receive [a bed] and lie down upon it while the senior monk is already sleeping?
The Buddha said:
“One should spread out bedding and then sit or lie down; there is no offense regarding what has been used previously.”
“As the World-Honored One has said, one must not cross by grasping a cow’s tail.
Is it permissible to cross by grasping the tail of another animal?
The Buddha said:
"Except for the tails of tigers, elephants, horses, and lions; if one grasps the tail of any other animal and crosses [a river], there is no offense.
"Is it permissible to accept molasses syrup for seven days?"
He replied:
"One may drink it.
For how long may one drink it?"
"Until its original nature has been discarded.
"If it is boiled together with impure medicinal ingredients, may it be eaten?
He replied:
"No. It may be used for anointing the body, for applying to a wound, or for nasal irrigation.
"If one cooks impure fat together with salt, is it permissible to eat it?"
He replied:
"It is not permitted.
However, if it were used as pig fat, there would be no offense."
“If a bhikṣu prepares the five kinds of seeds as pure by his own hand, using either a knife or his fingernails, is it considered purified?
Answer: “It is considered purified.”
“May it be eaten? “It may be eaten, provided it has been purified by fire.
If one kills grass for the sake of purifying it by fire, one commits a pāyattika offense.”
“If a tree stands on impure ground and its fruit falls onto pure ground, may it be eaten?
“It may be eaten provided it has not been kept overnight.
“If a tree stands on pure ground and its fruit falls onto impure ground, may it be eaten?”
He replied, "It is not permitted. [The questioner asked:
"If a *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible) is on impure ground, and performs the rite of making it pure on that impure ground, does it become pure?"
He replied,
“It is purified.
[The other asked,] “May it be eaten?”
“One may eat it, provided it has been purified by fire.
“If a person who purifies is on impure ground, and the purification is performed on pure ground, is it considered purified?
“It is considered purified.”
“May one eat it? “One may eat it, provided it has been purified by fire.
“May one eat eel meat?”
"No. "May one drink human milk?
"No, but it may be applied to the eyes."
“May *suvīra* juice be drunk outside of the proper time?
“It may be drunk by one who is ill.
“All impure meat is not to be eaten; may human flesh be eaten?”
"One must not eat it.
"What offense does one incur by eating it?

As the Buddha has taught, there is non-concordance regarding what is not Dharma, concordance regarding what is not Dharma, non-concordance regarding what is Dharma, and concordance regarding what is Dharma.

First, a formal announcement (*jñapti*) is made, and subsequently, the ritual act (*karman*) is performed; thus the Saṃgha is in concord.
That which is contrary to the above is termed discordance in accordance with the Dharma.
"If one bhikṣu expels one person, or many bhikṣus expel four persons, they commit a duṣkṛta offense.

There are two types of offenses: namely, those that last for a lifetime and those that are temporary.
There are two types of offenses: namely, those that are destroyed and those that are not destroyed.
There are two types of offenses: namely, light and heavy.
There are two types of offenses: namely, those with remainder and those without remainder.
